tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Bills > Summary Offences and Other Legislation Amendment (Public Assemblies) Bill 2025
tree_branches.text:
Debate resumed from an earlier hour.

The matter that I had not covered was section 87ZD (4), which gives some support to the powers that have been given to police in that, if there is a contravention of a direction by the police or if there is any resistance to police carrying out their actions under the subsection, then there are penalties that attach to that, being a maximum of 100 penalty units, which is an $11,000 fine or imprisonment for 12 months, or both. There is little point in giving the police those powers to stop people from disguising their identities unless there is some enforcement mechanism so that people will comply.

I explained schedule 1 and 2 to the bill. Schedule 2 [2] deals with the Supreme Court's decision in Lees v State of New South Wales and the striking down of section 200 (5) of the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act. The Government copied my amendment to that bill and put it in the Crimes Amendment (Places of Worship) Bill 2025 that passed the House yesterday. There is no need for me to explain that provision or to continue pushing that as part of the bill. It passed through the House thanks to the Government showing the greatest form of flattery—imitation—and copying my amendments, which solve the problems with Lees v State of New South Wales .

I encourage members to support the sensible reforms proposed in the bill. They are necessary to rebalance the public interest with regard to the Summary Offences Act and the provisions which make public assemblies lawful. They provide for a better balancing of the public interest in terms of giving protesters three free protests a year but, after that, making them pick up the tab for the police resources necessary to police them. Finally, schedule 2 to the bill deals with the undesirable nature of disguising appearance during public assemblies—which is endemic in extremist protests within our community, whether it be Nazis or others—from a law enforcement point of view and finds solutions to deal with that. I commend the bill to the House.

Debate adjourned.

The SPEAKER: There are many guests in the gallery today. I welcome you all to the Parliament of New South Wales for question time. I extend a very warm welcome to the Honorary Consul of Ukraine in Sydney, Kateryna Argyrou, and Nadia Mencinsky from the Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organisations. I imagine members will be looking forward to meeting you when the opportunity arises in the future. It is lovely to have you here today. I also warmly welcome Cole Young and Gina Young, who are foster carers; Bec Kennedy and Eli Kennedy, who are a foster family; Theresa Chen and Elicia Doty from Youth Consult for Change, which is a consultative group for young people experienced in out-of-home care; and Renee Leigh from Carers for Kids NSW. They are guests of the member for Port Stephens. I further welcome Leighton Drury, secretary of the Fire Brigade Employees Union, who is a guest of the member for Canterbury. Adam Hall will settle down—I will get to him.

I welcome members of the Sutherland Shire Preschool Alliance and the Independent Education Union from Cronulla Preschool, Engadine Preschool Kindergarten, The Point Preschool, Mayflower Preschool, Kurnell Pre School, Jannali Preschool Kindergarten, Uniting Preschool Caringbah, Jacaranda Preschool Caringbah, Miranda Kindergarten and Kurnell Pre School. They are guests of the member for Cronulla and the member for Miranda. I also welcome members of the Rotary Club of Chatswood Roseville, guests of the member for Davidson. I welcome members of the Bawley Point, Kioloa and Termeil Community Association, Lindsay Cane and Peter Longstaff, guests of the member for South Coast.

I welcome Adam Hall from the Health Services Union, guest of the member for Keira. I also welcome student leaders of Riverbank Public School and their principal, Jeannie Brown, guests of the member for Riverstone. I acknowledge Rose Harrison from St Phillip's Christian College, guest of the member for Newcastle. I also acknowledge Cobalt Walsh from Georges River Grammar School, guest of the member for East Hills. I welcome George Dolores and Tony Lentini, guests of the member for Castle Hill. I also welcome Marlin Rowe, guest of the member for Heathcote. I welcome Brett Wild, chairman of Taskforce Veteran, guest of the member for Hawkesbury. Finally, I acknowledge and welcome members of the Care Leavers Australasia Network, including CEO Leonie Sheedy, and students and teachers from Vincentia High School and The Forest High School. We welcome you to the Parliament. It is wonderful to have so many visitors today for question time.

tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Announcements > Legislative Council Order for Papers: Virtual Stock Fencing
tree_branches.text: The SPEAKER: I advise the House that on 22 October 2025 the Legislative Council made an order for papers relating to virtual fencing, including legislation on virtual fencing. The order has the potential to include documents held by government agencies that relate to proceedings in the Legislative Assembly and its committees. Consistent with the approach taken in relation to the Legislative Council's order for papers of 25 June concerning workers compensation legislation, documents captured by this order that relate to the proceedings of the Legislative Assembly will not be provided to the Legislative Council but instead provided to the Clerk on a confidential basis. Access to those documents will be restricted, with individual members permitted to inspect only correspondence involving themselves. Members are encouraged to contact the Clerk if they believe their correspondence is included, with the House ultimately deciding on broader access.

tree_branches.name: Parliament Smoke and Cigarette Free Policy
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Announcements > Parliament Smoke and Cigarette Free Policy
tree_branches.text: The SPEAKER ( 11:09 :56 ): I advise the House that the Parliament House Smoke and Cigarette Free Policy will be updated and formally implemented from January 2026 to ensure full compliance with the Smoke‑free Environment Act 2000. From 1 January, the updated policy will extend the existing restrictions to include vaping and electronic cigarettes as prohibited forms of smoking. It will also clarify the locations within the Parliamentary Precincts Act where smoking may be permitted under the Act. These changes follow an external review and site inspection, and are designed to provide a safe, healthy and compliant environment for all members, staff and visitors to the Parliament. A copy of the updated policy will be distributed by email shortly. I encourage all members and their staff to familiarise themselves with it.

Mr MARK SPEAKMAN ( Cronulla ) ( 11:12 :29 ): My question is directed to the Premier. Community preschool educators join us in the gallery today. They earn up to 30 per cent less than teachers in schools doing similar work, and around 15 per cent less than staff in long day care. Families trust their children with these people every day. Why will the Government not fund a fair pay rise for the incredible work they do?

The SPEAKER: Members will come to order.

Mr CHRIS MINNS ( Kogarah — Premier ) ( 11:13 :08 ): That concern from the industry would have been welcomed when the Opposition was in government. The truth is that over the 12 years that the previous Government was in power there was record low investment in that area of public spending. The former Liberal‑Nationals Government did not build a single public preschool in New South Wales in 12 years. As a result, there is a massive differential between the number of private providers and public and community providers in Victoria versus New South Wales. Most of the childcare deserts in our State are funded by private providers because there are no public providers. As a result, the Government has stepped into the breach and announced the largest early childhood education investment, which includes 100 new preschools in the State, 49 of which will be in regional New South Wales. The reason for that is straightforward.

Ms Eleni Petinos: Point of order—

The SPEAKER: The Clerk will stop the clock.

Ms Eleni Petinos: My point of order relates to Standing Order 129. The Premier was asked about preschool workers' pay, not bricks and mortar.

The SPEAKER: There is no point of order. The Premier was being directly relevant. The Premier has the call.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: That goes to my point. Under the Coalition, there were no preschools to fund—none, zero—because its members did not build a single preschool. The community sector is underpaid.

The SPEAKER: Members will come to order.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: After 12 years of the former Government putting virtually nothing into the sector, this Government has made the decision to build 100 public preschools.

The SPEAKER: The Leader of the Opposition will come to order. I call the member for North Shore to order for the first time.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: We are working with the community sector and unions to provide pay at the appropriate levels.

The SPEAKER: I call the Leader of the Opposition to order for the first time.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: After three years in opposition the Coalition has offered nothing in the way of a policy prescription, yet its members ask, "Where have you been for the past three years?" I ask Opposition members where were they in the decade before that?

The SPEAKER: I will not tolerate members shouting across the Chamber after the Premier has resumed his seat. It is disorderly. Members will be respectful of each other in the Chamber.

Mr WARREN KIRBY ( Riverstone ) ( 11:15 :24 ): My question is addressed to the Premier. Will the Premier outline the challenges to our renewable energy transition?

Mr CHRIS MINNS ( Kogarah — Premier ) ( 11:15 :35 ): I refer the House to an article in The Sydney Morning Herald from yesterday entitled, "'Sad': Bank chief slams Australia's political failure on net zero and energy." It stated:

One of the nation's leading bankers says … the nation's failure to resolve its political impasse over energy [is] a sad development that should never have happened.

Mr Michael Kemp: Bank chief? Do we trust them with our profits?

Mr CHRIS MINNS: I would love to hear what Opposition members have to say. They are welcome to move a motion; otherwise, they are just interrupting.

[ Opposition members interjected. ]

Honestly, can I not get out an answer?

The SPEAKER: Members will come to order.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: The article stated:

NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said more renewables and natural gas in the power grid would ensure the country could meet its net zero commitments while maintaining its industrial base.

Let us go through that again—"more renewables and natural gas in the power grid". Renewable energy firmed with gas seems to be the New South Wales Government's policy. The Narrabri expansion is a big part of that. Given that Narrabri is located in a Nationals electorate, one would think the incoming Leader of The Nationals would have a view about that.

The SPEAKER: The member for Upper Hunter will come to order.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: Yesterday the member for Coffs Harbour was asked about that by Laura Jayes on Sky News.

Mr Mark Speakman: Point of order—

The SPEAKER: The Clerk will stop the clock.

Mr Mark Speakman: My point of order relates to Standing Order 129. The Premier keeps talking about the Opposition, but why is he failing to meet his own interim targets?

The SPEAKER: There is no point of order. The Leader of the Opposition will resume his seat.

Mr Ron Hoenig: Point of order: My point of order relates to Standing Order 131 (8), which makes it very clear that members cannot take points of order simply to interrupt proceedings. Two baseless points of order have already been taken. The Leader of the Opposition should know better than that. Mr Speaker, I ask that you firmly enforce Standing Order 131 (8) and stop these needless, baseless points of order from being taken.

Mr Mark Speakman: To the point of order: The question was about challenges to the renewables transition.

The SPEAKER: Members will not debate the question. I heard and understood the point of order taken by the Leader of the House. I do not uphold it. I do not require assistance from members. At this point I will not take action against the Leader of the Opposition. He will resume his seat. I will not tolerate members taking points of order simply to interfere with the flow of proceedings. The Premier has the call.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: Laura Jayes asked the new Leader of the National Party, "Is part of the solution Narrabri?" The National Party has said, "We're not for net zero. We're out."

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Coffs Harbour to order for the first time.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: One would have thought that was a reasonably simple question, but the Leader of the National Party said, "I admit that I don't yet have a position on Narrabri because, certainly, I'm pretty fresh into the role." Laura Jayes says, "I find that a bit unusual. We were talking about that this morning. Certainly you have considered Narrabri? Certainly you have considered gas? You wouldn't have taken on the position of National Party leader unless you had thought about it?" And he says, "As a junior MP, I was focused on my seat. As deputy leader, I was focused on other things."

We know what he was focusing on—getting rid of his boss, not policy issues in New South Wales. Is that unfair or will the record bear that out? I am willing to bet that the record will bear that out. What did Dugald say on the way out the door? "I hope you get what's coming to you." That is what the NAB has said and that is what Dugald said. But in the past week one leader has stood up and pushed an important stake in the ground on net zero and the energy transition, and that is the Leader of the Opposition. He played a blinder this morning. Whacking questions out of the park on 2GB and 702. [ Extension of time ]

I thought he was unreal—a little bit like Greg Chappell hitting 100 in his final innings. I was interested in the position he came up with. He said, "We're going to do net zero." He got that through the party room of the Liberal Party. I have been giving the National Party a hard time, but where are the Liberal Party on net zero? The Hon. Rachel Merton in the upper House came out and said, "I don't support net zero and"—interestingly—"at least 10 of my colleagues echo that sentiment." Who are those 10 colleagues?

Mr James Griffin: Point of order—

The SPEAKER: The Clerk will stop the clock. I am sure the Premier was asking a rhetorical question. I will hear the point of order.

Mr James Griffin: My point of order is about the looseness of members of the Legislative Council. We should not pay much credit to what they say.

The SPEAKER: That is a popular point of order, but I do not uphold it. The member for Manly will resume his seat. The Premier will continue his answer.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: That is a risky thing to say when in the middle of a leadership ballot—"Ignore the upper House". They do get a vote. I have an article from a Tim James—I think it is the same Tim James as the member for Willoughby. It is from 2018. He says, "It also points to the absurdity of their position which is to lock in for net zero emissions by 2050." That is what he said in an article for the Menzies Research Centre. It may not be the same Tim James. I do not know. I assume it is him.

Mr Tim James: How many years ago?

Mr CHRIS MINNS: It is time dependent, apparently. I give the House an updated quote. This is what he said last week. The Daily Telegraph said to him, "There was a position at a Liberal Party branch meeting this weekend and you abstained. Why did you abstain?" I have the response. It says, "Mr James was approached by the Telegraph and he said he would await the position of the Federal party before commenting on the target." He is outsourcing his brain to Barnaby Joyce and Sussan Ley. Is that the plan? He has gone to New York, he has an MBA and he has travelled around the world, but he comes to State Parliament and lets the Feds take over.

The SPEAKER: The member for Willoughby will come to order.

Mr JAMES GRIFFIN ( Manly ) ( 11:23 :15 ): My question is directed to the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces. Will the Minister finally come clean and tell the people of New South Wales how much it will really cost to deliver his plan to slash Moore Park Golf Course in half?

Mr Ron Hoenig: Point of order—

The SPEAKER: Members will come to order or leave the Chamber. I will hear the Leader of the House on a point of order.

Mr Ron Ho enig: The member for Manly knows how to ask a question in accordance with Standing Order 128 (3). He should ask his question again so it does not contain argument, inference or imputation. Alternatively, the next member should be called to ask a question.

The SPEAKER: I uphold the point of order taken by the Leader of the House. The member for Manly has an opportunity to repair the question so that it is in order.

Mr JAMES GRIFFIN: I will tee off again, minus the argumentative element. My question is directed to the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces. Will the Minister tell the people of New South Wales how much it will cost to deliver the plan to cut Moore Park Golf Course in half?

The SPEAKER: That is how you do it. Members will come to order.

Mr PAUL SCULLY ( Wollongong — Minister for Planning and Public Spaces ) ( 11:25 :00 ): The member for Manly shanked the first question, and it did not get any better the second time. He has put it right in the drink with this one. He cannot play himself out of a bad run. He is not on the leaderboard any more, is he? He is not troubling the scorers over there, is he?

The SPEAKER: Members will come to order.

Mr PAUL SCULLY: I refer the member to the budget. Some $50 million has been allocated to deliver a 20-hectare park at Moore Park.

Mr Kevin Anderson: It's already a park.

Mr PAUL SCULLY: The member for Tamworth should look after Scully Park. It is the best park he has got. The Government committed $50 million in the last budget to deliver a 20-hectare park at Moore Park, which will be delivered within three years.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Wahroonga to order for the first time.

Mr PAUL SCULLY: The park will include a community sporting field, a community football field, multipurpose sports courts, a playground, walking and cycling paths, and biodiversity enhancements. Given the member is so interested in the future of Moore Park, I encourage him to have his say through the public exhibition process that is currently underway. All members can have their say and all people in the gallery can have their say, if they are interested, until 24 November. So get in quick.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Terrigal to order for the first time.

Mr PAUL SCULLY: The member for Manly should stop counting the numbers. Do not count that scorecard. He should worry about his golf scorecard. He can get in and have his say, too. We would particularly like to hear as part of the exhibition process, because I know he is so interested, what his priorities are in addition to those things—such as where he thinks off‑leash dog areas might go, where we might put outdoor fitness facilities, where a pump track and youth recreation facilities might go, how the perimeter loop track might be done, and what the spaces for passive recreation might look like. The Government is determined to deliver more public open space.

Mr Mark Speakman: Point of order: The question was about cost. We have heard how much is in the budget and what the project is going to be. How much will it actually cost?

The SPEAKER: I thank the Leader of the Opposition. I do not uphold the point of order. The Minister is being directly relevant.

Mr PAUL SC ULLY: I appreciate that this week the Leader of the Opposition is struggling with numbers, so I will say it again for him: $50 million is committed in the budget to be delivered over three years. It will provide additional public space in an area that is already one of the most densely populated in Sydney and is set to grow by 100,000 people in the coming years.

Ms KYLIE WILKINSON ( East Hills ) ( 11:27 :46 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Health. Will the Minister please update the House on how the Minns Labor Government is building health infrastructure to support the growing needs of Western Sydney?

Mr RYAN PARK ( Keira — Minister for Health, Minister for Regional Health, and Minister for the Illawarra a nd the South Coast ) ( 11:27 :58 ): I thank the member for East Hills. She is an incredible advocate. Because of her advocacy, the people of Bankstown and the East Hills electorate will receive the largest investment in a public hospital in the history of the State—$2 billion right in the heart of western and south-western Sydney. That is crucially needed. The member for East Hills has been a strong advocate alongside many other local members in this place for that important local hospital. I thank her and the team for that. The hospital was delayed for too long simply because the Opposition when in government could not select a site. I do not understand why it took so long, but it did. The site was argued about and debated up hill and down dale. When we took over, I wanted to select a site and get on with it straight away. We had to increase that budget to the tune of about $700 million because those delays had led to cost escalation. People in Bankstown and the surrounding area would not have gotten the hospital they need and deserve. Our priority now, with the concept designs released, is cracking on and building that hospital as quickly as we can.

We are also building the hospital at Rouse Hill, which those opposite know well because they took it to three elections. That is not bad. I am assuming they know it very well. But the difference between us and them is we are actually building it, with an emergency department and with maternity and birthing units. The member for Riverstone has been a terrific advocate for that. He was doorknocking in the area and that was arguably one of the biggest issues that that growing part of north‑western Sydney faced. He reported back to me and what we were clearly getting from the community was that the hospital needed to be bigger in scale and size. That is why we made a decision to triple the size of the investment into that hospital. Over $900 million is now going into that part of north-west Sydney to deliver a hospital that the community needs and deserves.

But it does not stop there. We are also investing heavily into two hospitals that have not been upgraded for many decades: Canterbury Hospital and Fairfield Hospital. Those two hospitals desperately needed investment. Fairfield will get an investment of $550 million. I thank all the local MPs, who have been terrific advocates alongside their local community members, as well as hospital staff. They were saying for some time, "We're simply outgrowing the hospital that we have." [ Extension of time ]

I thank those local MPs, as well as those who have advocated for Canterbury Hospital, which has received an investment of $350 million. That hospital is loved by many in that local community, in a very multicultural part of Sydney. It has been their local community hospital for a long time. In addition, we are also investing in the men and women who deliver the health services that we desperately need. I acknowledge Adam Hall from the Health Services Union [HSU], who is in the gallery today. I announce that before Christmas over 50,000 HSU members—many of whom are the lowest paid health workers in New South Wales—are going to receive a substantial increase in their pay. That has been advocated for and fought for by the Health Services Union, and delivered by a government that removed the wages cap. It would not have been possible under the Coalition because of its obsession with the wages cap.

The Health Services Union has advocated for the individuals who keep our hospitals clean, who keep the kitchens in our hospitals operating, who make sure that we are safe—through the security teams in our local hospitals—and who do all of the administration, admission and discharge paperwork to ensure that we get into and leave our hospitals as safely and efficiently as we possibly can. Those people often go unnoticed in our hospital system. But they do not go unnoticed by members on this side of the Chamber. Without them, we would not be able to open the doors of our hospitals every day. I hope all those union members enjoy that pay rise. They deserve it and fought for it. We cannot wait to give them more.

Mr ALEX GREENWICH ( Sydney ) ( 11:33 :42 ): My question is directed to the Minister for Police and Counter-terrorism. I acknowledge that today is Trans Day of Remembrance and this morning I joined with the NSW Police Force and the trans community to see the trans pride flag raised over the Sydney Police Centre. How is the NSW Police Force working to improve its relationship with the LGBTQ+ community and improve the community's safety on Oxford Street and across New South Wales?

Ms YASMIN CATLEY ( Swansea — Minister for Police and Counter-terrorism, and Minister for the Hunter ) ( 11:34 :09 ): I thank the member for Sydney for his question. I am pleased that he was able to commemorate today at the police centre. We have come a long way and I am proud to be able to give the member a response. The relationship between the LGBTQIA+ community and police is an incredibly important one. Both the NSW Police Force and the Government acknowledge that that relationship has had a fraught history. But it has strengthened over the years and the police continue to work every day towards making it even better.

As we approach the Mardi Gras 2026 season and the upcoming anniversary of the Special Commission of Inquiry into LGBTIQ hate crimes, it is a good time to reflect on the journey of the NSW Police Force and how it works with the LGBTQIA+ community, and its efforts to make sure that police create a safe space for all victims of crime. Many of those efforts are concentrated in and around the inner city and the Oxford Street entertainment precinct, which is in the electorate of the member for Sydney. We know that that neighbourhood is one where many LGBTQIA+ community members can feel, and have felt, their safest. To make sure the neighbourhood can be free from violence, hate and discrimination, local police deploy a high‑visibility, prevention‑focused presence on Oxford Street every Friday and Saturday night.

They are also engaging with the Oxford Street Rainbow Precinct and working collaboratively with businesses who are signatories to the Oxford Street Pride Charter. Those are important steps in the journey to being granted the internationally recognised Purple Flag accreditation for the precinct. We want Oxford Street to be safe, fun and vibrant. The good news is that our hard work is showing results. I am pleased to report that 80 per cent of all alcohol‑related assaults within the Surry Hills command result in legal action. That is significantly high—in fact, it is the highest rate of all commands—and alcohol‑related assaults have dropped by 20 per cent, making the area safer for all, especially our LGBTQIA+ community. But it is not just about Oxford Street. We recognise that the LGBTQIA+ community is a diverse one, one that exists and has always existed across every corner of the State of New South Wales. It is a community not bound by faith, ethnicity or culture, but by who they love. [ Extension of time ]

Sadly, the community is vulnerable to discrimination, marginalisation, prejudice and hate. We know there are additional barriers to members of the community seeking justice and we recognise that, in the past, police have been complicit in those barriers. For that, we are deeply sorry. Our gender diverse and LGBTQIA+ liaison officers, commonly and warmly known as GLLOs, are one of our most important bridges to the community. I am so proud of the work that they do engaging with the community day in, day out. Our Engagement and Hate Crime Unit also provides education and training to police on hate crimes and reviews incidents that police officers record as hate crimes.

We also have to talk about the Special Commission of Inquiry into LGBTIQ hate crimes and the action we are taking as a result of it. The inquiry made 19 recommendations, 15 of which were directed at the police. All have been supported. The NSW Police Force has already completed several recommendations, and reinvestigations have already occurred in relation to the deaths of Gerald Cuthbert and Kenneth Brennan. Police have committed to regularly running DNA profiles against DNA databases should new evidence become available. Our LGBTQIA+ Consultative Committee provides a forum for community consultation in the development of police responses to the inquiry's recommendations. I thank the member for Sydney for his participation in that committee as New South Wales police continue to build their relationship with the LGBTQIA+ community and improve community safety outcomes on Oxford Street and beyond. Both the police and the Government are determined to build a future where every LGBTQIA+ person feels safe, respected and protected.

Ms JENNY LEONG ( Newtown ) ( 12:08 :48 ): My question is directed to Minister for Planning and Public Spaces. The Inner West Council is currently considering a development application to convert a block of four apartments, previously used as housing for people seeking asylum, into a single mansion. Will the Minister work with me to update State planning rules to include "no net dwelling loss" provisions, similar to those already in place in local government areas like the City of Sydney, to ensure that housing supply cannot be reduced by developments in this way?

Mr PAUL SCULLY ( Wollongong — Minister for Planning and Public Spaces ) ( 12:09 :25 ): I thank the member for Newtown for her question. I am pleased to have a question from the member today about the ways we can make sure that there are as many homes as possible in all parts of the State. In answer to the substance of her question, let me say upfront that I am happy to work with any member on sensible ideas about how to increase housing supply. I think I have demonstrated that multiple times including by the fact that we have had near‑universal support for planning reforms through this Parliament over the past week. I am pleased that the City of Sydney has finalised its changes regarding no net dwelling loss and that it has been able to finalise a plan that works for its local area. No net dwelling loss is an issue that can be particularly localised, and it is important in that regard that councils play a key role in determining those policies where they influence their local communities.

I understand that Waverley and Woollahra councils have also considered introducing a similar policy approach. I am having a look at those to make sure they are not actually anti-housing. Some councils use some of these mechanisms to curb supply rather than encourage it. I am aware that the Inner West Council has also done some work to introduce a no net dwelling loss policy as part of its recently finalised Fairer Future Plan changes. I congratulate Mayor Byrne and the Inner West councillors on getting that work done and supporting more homes in their local community. It is important that all parts of the State play their role.

I appreciate the concern of the member for Newtown, shared by many members in this place, about the ongoing affordability and availability of housing in New South Wales, particularly in their own communities. As I said earlier, we have to make sure that some of these changes, when introduced, do not have a chilling effect or an anti-supply effect in terms of increasing the overall level of supply. The simple fact when it comes to housing affordability is that we are going to need more supply. The situation is that for decades we simply have not been building enough homes in New South Wales. That is what has driven up prices and rents. Add to that the fact that the previous Government sold off large swathes of social housing, meaning even less homes were available for those on low and moderate incomes.

That is the reality we face and that we are going to have to deal with. We understand that if you do not build more homes, there is no chance of New South Wales or any part of Sydney remaining a place where everyone can afford to live. That is why we have continued to undertake reforms. We took steps to increase the supply of all types of market housing, as well as increasing the supply of affordable housing. The Government's infill affordable housing bonus has been doing exactly that since it was introduced in December 2023. I guess the member does not want additional information, so I will leave it there.

Ms MARYANNE ST UART ( Heathcote ) ( 11:46 :48 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Work Health and Safety. Will the Minister update the House on the Government's work to address skyrocketing workers compensation premiums in New South Wales?

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS ( Canterbury — Minister for Industrial Relations, and Minister for Work Health and Safety ) ( 11:47 :11 ): I thank the amazing member for Heathcote. This morning we were joined by the owners of hundreds of wonderful small businesses from her area in the electorate of the member for Miranda, at Tradies. They do an incredible job. I also thank the president of the Sutherland Shire Business Chamber, Jeanne Zweck, who spoke so eloquently and passionately about the devastation that will come to small and medium‑size businesses. I will share a part of what Jeanne said this morning:

Businesses are hurting. … If you're running a small business, you want to be planning for the year ahead. If your premium goes up by $10,000, how do you plan for that? Another case where business premiums have gone up by 30 per cent. How do you plan to keep doors open when you can't plan for these amounts—those increases? We need the dialogue to come together and have a resolution so that it is better for business. In Caringbah … There are "for lease" signs everywhere. Businesses can't plan and service levels are being impacted because they have to find the funds in order to function.

That is what businesses are saying. I also acknowledge John Lamont, the president of the Shoalhaven Business Chamber, which is in the electorate of the member for South Coast. He was on radio this week. He is a strong advocate for the changes. I also acknowledge the other business chambers—including the Campbelltown Chamber of Commerce, which the Premier and the Treasurer visited—that have expressed their concerns about that lot opposite deserting small and medium-sized businesses. One in five will hit the wall because of them. Members opposite do not believe in small businesses. The Government knows that small businesses are the lifeblood of the State's economy, contributing $535 billion annually.

In June this year an anonymous MP quoted in The Daily Telegraph said, "If we don't stand for small business, who do we stand for?" Those opposite do not know who they stand for. That is the wrong approach and politically stupid. Behind the scenes they say, and in my ear they tell me, "We've really stuffed up this, so keep going as hard as you can." That is what they are telling me. Liberal Party members I spoke to on the South Coast said, "We can't believe what they're doing." Menzies would be rolling in his grave because of what those opposite have done. They have failed to stand up and publicly state their position. They do not know what it is themselves. Liberal members are coming to me and asking, "What's all this about?" On ABC radio the former small business Minister said, "I've sat in rooms with Business NSW, chambers and clubs, the Pharmacy Guild and GPs—[ Extension of time ]

The former small business Minister sat in rooms with GPs, not-for-profits, charities, the artistic community and the Association of Independent Schools. All were concerned. Everybody agrees—even those opposite—that the system is broken with respect to psychosocial claims. Businesses, charities, GPs and independent schools are saying to us, "Please come together and fix this so that we can get on with business." But those opposite have chosen a political pathway that will not get them where they want to be. Instead, they will see businesses shut and "For Lease" signs. One in five businesses will hit the wall, and they are making decisions now about cutting staff and services. Last week when the Legislative Council debated those reforms for 16 hours the Opposition had the chance to be on the side of businesses and the not-for-profits. Instead, it chose to be on the side of premium increases of 17 per cent, which will affect 340,00 businesses over the next year.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Albury to order for the first time.

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS: That sits on Opposition members' shoulders because they did nothing for 10 years—absolutely nothing. They did not manage claims properly. They did not manage psychosocial claims. Those who held the portfolio had the data. They knew what was happening and what was coming. They could see the trend, but they chose to do absolutely nothing. We are cleaning up their mess. Those opposite are not the party of small business; we are the party of small business. The Minister for Small Business is doing an amazing job. The Liberals are the party of job cuts, staff cuts and "For Lease" signs across New South Wales

The SPEAKER: The member for Wollongong has brought to my attention that Arthur Rorris, Secretary of the South Coast Labour Council, is in the public gallery. I welcome him to the Legislative Assembly.

Ms STEPH COOKE ( Cootamundra ) ( 11:52 :57 ): My question is directed to the Minister for Recovery. Lismore is still recovering from the 2022 floods. One major infrastructure project that the community is still waiting for is the complete refurbishment and rebuild of the sewage treatment plant in East Lismore. Will the Minister commit to fully funding and delivering this project?

Ms JANELLE SAFFIN ( Lismore — Minis ter for Small Business, Minister for Recovery, and Minister for the North Coast ) ( 11:53 :24 ): I thank the member for Cootamundra for her question. She probably knows this project as well as I do. I was with the member for Tamworth, the then Minister, when we announced the project onsite. Some $145 million was made available to the seven councils across the Northern Rivers, but there has been debate and argy-bargy about which councils will do what. Some councils want to build to betterment and projected population growth in the area. However, this was not considered in the announcement and has partly contributed to the delay. I am well aware of the Lismore project. The mayor and I have differing recollections about it, but we are dealing with it. It will get done.

Mrs SALLY QUINNELL ( Camden ) ( 11:54 :34 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Roads. Will the Minister please update the House on the Minns Labor Government's investment in critical road links across New South Wales?

Ms JENNY AITCHISON ( Maitland — Minister for Regional Transport, and Minister for Roads ) ( 11:54 :56 ): I have a lot to get through, so it would be great if the House could be a little quieter so I do not have to yell.

The SPEAKER: The Minister's colleagues will be quiet also.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: I thank the member for Camden. She is a hardworking member and strong advocate for her electorate. She raises issues around congestion and safety on behalf of her community all the time. I am pleased to share with the member and the House that today we announced two proposed new signalised intersections on Remembrance Driveway. We have visited that site. I thank the member for advocating not only for her electorate but also for all of south-western Sydney. She is a one of the many leading lights on this side of the House—there are a few on the crossbench as well—who really push for better infrastructure.

We are coming to the end of the year. Far be it from me to play Mrs Claus, but I want to reflect on some of our Government's roads and regional transport achievements across New South Wales. I will not say we have done it all from A to Z, but it is pretty close. I have a short list. In the Auburn and Granville electorates we are close to completing the Cumberland traffic study. In the Albury electorate we are developing a corridor strategy for the full length of the Hume Highway. The member for Badgerys Creek can thank us for the Elizabeth Drive upgrade—we have done that for her. We have improved the Bruxner Highway and Ballina Road intersection in the Ballina electorate and upgraded the Balmain East Sea Wall in the Balmain electorate. In the Bankstown and Canterbury electorates we have delivered major maintenance works along key bus corridors, including Canterbury Road.

In Barwon, we have sealed the Cobb Highway and are now working on Rangari Road. For the member for Bathurst—he has moved up this year; he is not quite in the top job yet, but he will get there—we have worked on the Great Western Highway. For the member for Bega, we are working on the Cuttagee Bridge and have improved the Tuross Head intersection, making the Princes Highway safer. We have widened Richmond Road in the Blacktown electorate and are planning an upgrade at Bungarribee Road. In the Blue Mountains electorate we are delivering an upgrade of Medlow Bath and improvements along the Bells Line of Road for the member for Hawkesbury. They did not put her on the release. That was really sad.

The SPEAKER: There is too much audible conversation in the Chamber. Members should be listening intently to the Minister.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: In Cabramatta, we delivered the Horsley Drive upgrade and improvements to school crossings. In Campbelltown, we upgraded Appin Road.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Clarence to order for the first time.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: In Cessnock, we paid natural disaster claims to the member's council in Singleton. In Charlestown, we improved Hillsborough Road. We picked up the Coffs Harbour Bypass project that had been ignored for so long. The work done prior to 2021 was delayed for nearly a decade, but we are steaming ahead. The member for Coffs Harbour can just say thank you. In Coogee, we provided millions of dollars in Get NSW Active grants for safer walking and cycling infrastructure. In Cootamundra, we fixed the level crossing. I remember in 2021 when we were in opposition that was going to be fixed next week, but we have finished it.

The SPEAKER: The member for Oatley will resume his seat.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: In Davidson, we installed new pedestrian crossings. In Drummoyne, we fixed the Australia Avenue roundabout.

Mrs Sally Quinnell: As the Minister is only up to the letter D, I seek further information.

The SPEAKER: An additional two minutes is granted. I am hoping for more.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: In Dubbo, we delivered the new Dubbo Bridge. In East Hills, we widened Henry Lawson Drive and upgraded Yeramba Lagoon. In Epping, we upgraded Epping Bridge. In Fairfield, we upgraded The Horsely Drive. We delivered new sections of the Gosford Bypass and the New Richmond Bridge in Hawkesbury. We delivered a beautiful upgrade of Heathcote Road—a legacy of the former member Alison Megarrity. In Heffron, we upgraded Sydney Park Junction. In Hornsby, we made Bridge Road and George Street safer. In Keira, we are building the Mount Ousley interchange.

The SPEAKER: I direct the member for Holsworthy to remove herself from the Chamber under Standing Order 249A.

[ Interruption ]

Order! I direct the Serjeant‑at‑Arms to remove the member for Holsworthy from the building under Standing Order 249.

[ Th e member for Holsworthy left the Chamber at 11:59 accompanied by the Serjeant ‑at ‑Arms . ]

If members are directed to leave the Chamber under Standing Order 249A and continue to interject, they will be removed for the day. It is not that hard. The Premier will come to order. The Minister has the call.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: At Windsor Road in Rouse Hill, the infrastructure was never built when those opposite were in government—it was imaginary infrastructure. We are getting on with it now. Kiama and Jervis Bay are getting upgrades; amazing work is happening on Tripoli Way. The Speers Point roundabout in the Speaker's electorate of Lake Macquarie is getting an upgrade. In Lane Cove—where is the member for Lane Cove today? Is he doing the numbers? Where is the member for Epping?

Mr Adam Crouch: She's at a funeral, by the way, in case you wanted to know.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: I'm sorry about that. Leppington has the Fifteenth Avenue upgrade. Lismore has the Alphadale Road intersection; we are getting that upgraded.

The SPEAKER: It is the last question time of the year, and we are all getting excited. Members will come to order. I call the member for Miranda.

Ms ELENI PET INOS ( Miranda ) ( 12:00 :45 ): My question is directed to the Minister for Work Health and Safety. Will the Minister finally come clean and tell the people of New South Wales that she could keep workers compensation premiums down but just does not want to?

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS ( Canterbury — Minister for Industrial Relations, and Minister for Work Health and Safety ) ( 12:01 :08 ): That is a great Dixer for the last question time. I acknowledge the hardworking workers in the gallery. I thank them, as well as Adam Hall and Leighton Drury, for the terrific work that they do.

Mr Mark Speakman: By slashing their benefits?

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS: No, you slashed their benefits.

The SPEAKER: Members will come to order.

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS: It is because those opposite were asleep at the wheel. They did nothing for 10 years. The McDougall report came out and they were embarrassed into taking some action, starting to do the reforms to icare.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Wahroonga to order for the second time.

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS: We had to come in and open the books, and it was a complete mess. We brought a number of reforms into this place and those opposite were embarrassed. We had to drag them in here, kicking and screaming, to make the changes to icare. More importantly, those opposite took no action when it came to the trends in psychosocial claims. Now small- and medium-sized businesses, without a single claim, will face a 17 per cent rise in premiums because of those opposite. They did absolutely nothing. They were not involved in any round tables. They did not come to the table. Every single business—

Ms Eleni Petinos: Point of order: My point of order is taken under Standing Order 129. The Minister was specifically asked about the exercise of her powers to keep premiums low.

The SPEAKER: I will rule on the point of order. The Minister has some discretion in answering the question because it was out of order under Standing Order 128 (2) (b) and (c), and probably a few other standing orders. I will hear no further points of order under Standing Order 129. The Minister has the call.

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS: I take very seriously what the shadow Minister has said about the powers of the Minister with respect to icare. The board makes their decision. But ultimately, at the end of the day, we need to have a sustainable scheme for the hard workers of New South Wales. Some 340,000 businesses will be impacted because of the decision by those opposite. They will be paying in their own electorates, whether it is the electorate of Winston Hills, Badgerys Creek or the shadow Minister's electorate of Miranda. In the electorate of the Leader of the Opposition, every second or third shop in Caringbah has a For Lease sign. The chambers of commerce have been doorknocking their offices, asking and pleading for them to do the right thing. They have let down small businesses. When they do that, they let down workers, prospective workers and apprentices, because there is no certainty and no guarantee of those jobs.

Mr NATHAN HAGARTY ( Leppington ) ( 12:04 :15 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Skills, TAFE and Tertiary Education, representing the Minister for Education and Early Learning. Will the Minister update the House on the Minns Labor Government's record investment in new schools and upgrades, ensuring that families have access to world-class public education?

Mr STEVE WHAN ( Monaro — Minister for Skills, TAFE and Tertiary Education ) ( 12:04 :38 ): I thank the member for Leppington for his question. What a great question from our side of the House to highlight the work that we have done this year in delivering for the people of New South Wales, and how different that is to the work of those opposite. It is close to Christmas, but today's grab bag from Opposition members felt like they did not know what they were unwrapping when they got up to ask their questions. They were all over the place. The member for Leppington has had a firsthand view of the way school development is happening in his area. We are delivering a new high school at Leppington. I understand the concrete pour has just got underway for the main part of the building. It is fantastic work. At Emerald Hills, we are building a new primary school with a public preschool. I understand there is a community information session planned for that in a couple of weeks.

The work in Leppington is part of the biggest school infrastructure program in New South Wales history, delivered from a record $9 billion, which is $400 million more than when the former Government left office. I stress that we are delivering on those projects. A number of the answers heard today were about the number of projects that Opposition members announced and turned a sod on but that did not get underway. Education is no different. They thought they would just put out a media release or some lines and somehow the school would miraculously appear. Under the leadership of the Deputy Premier, we have reformed school infrastructure. The planning Minister has reformed the planning system, and the Government has cut red tape so that a record 230 new schools, public preschools or upgrades are either in construction or about to commence. That is 39 new schools, including the first high school in the Hills since Labor was last in government.

The difference between our Government and those opposite can be summed up by the $230 million upgrade at Carlingford West Public School and Cumberland High School. That upgrade was promised to the electorate of Epping back in 2018. I am disappointed the member for Epping is not here today. Earlier this year I welcomed her to the second‑generation politicians club, which I and some others are members of. But, I have to say, I would be very embarrassed if work was only just starting—some five years later—on something that my dad had announced. Thankfully, the Minns Government was elected and we got that project moving. We have now delivered the $230 million upgrade, replacing 130 ageing demountables—most of them put there by Opposition members—with permanent classrooms. I wish that we could give the Liberals credit for that. If they had taken action, the classrooms would have been built years ago. Two weeks ago Cabinet went out to Camden, where the Premier and the acting Minister visited Gledswood Hills and Gregory Hills. That community had to beg the then schools Minister, and the member for Camden can tell members about the lengths the parents had to go to.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Mr Speaker—

The SPEAKER: The member for Leppington missed the jump. The Minister's time has expired. As we have saved two minutes, I take the opportunity to remind all members on behalf of the member for Summer Hill that the Parliamentary Friends of Cricket will meet on level 9 immediately after question time. Howzat! I call the member for Newtown.

Ms SONIA HORNERY ( Wallsend ) ( 12:12 :36 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Families and Communities. Will the Minister please update the House on work being undertaken by the Minns Labor Government to recruit more foster carers to care for vulnerable children and young people?

Ms KATE WASHINGTON ( Port Stephens — Minister for Families and Communities, and Minister for Disabili ty Inclusion ) ( 12:12 :53 ): I thank the hardworking member for Wallsend, who is a true champion for her community. I think it is entirely appropriate that we end the last question time for 2025 with a question about one of the real priorities for our Government, which is vulnerable children and families. It is an area where we have been getting on with the job and doing the difficult work of cleaning up the mess that those opposite left us. Foster carers do an extraordinary job. When children and young people cannot live safely with their families, foster carers are there, opening their hearts and their homes to kids who need it most. Every day thousands of people in our communities step up and provide a loving home for vulnerable children who have already seen too much instability. I welcome a number of important guests in the gallery today, being foster carers, care leavers and the CEO of Carers for Kids NSW, Renee Carter. We thank them for being here today.

We want to see more people changing a child's life by becoming a foster carer, because there are still far too many children not growing up in safe and loving home environments. As we all know, the Liberals and The Nationals left us with a broken child protection system that was spiralling out of control. They neglected out‑of‑home care for more than a decade and decided to outsource foster care recruitment—the very people we rely on as critical partners in child protection. What was the result? The former Government was responsible for the worst foster carer shortage in living memory. Without foster carers, the child protection system was pushed to breaking point, reliant on placing children in entirely unacceptable arrangements like hotels, motels and caravan parks with unaccredited providers. These were awful conditions for some of the State's most vulnerable children.

In April this year the New South Wales Government banned unaccredited providers. When we came to government, there were hundreds of children cycling through these arrangements and now there are none. I am pleased to advise the House of the next steps in the Government's reforms. Today we are launching a statewide foster carer recruitment campaign urging the people of New South Wales to change a child's life by becoming a foster carer like Bec, who is here today with her son, Eli. She is a strong advocate for foster caring for sibling groups particularly. I met Eli this morning and he is an impressive young man who has grown up in a foster carer family and has a compassionate soul already. If there is anyone here who knows more about the importance of foster caring, it is Theresa, a care leaver, who is also in the gallery today. [ Extension of time ]

Despite the instability she experienced during her time in care, Theresa is finishing her first degree today—and another is to come. Her message today was really clear. She said that we need carers urgently. She said:

By committing to being a carer, you're committing to promising better outcomes and a better future for every child and young person that goes through the child protection system.

There are no more powerful words than that from someone who knows first-hand the importance of the campaign we are launching today. We know that many people in New South Wales would consider becoming a carer but remain hesitant because of some myths around fostering and eligibility. Many people do not know that you can foster children if you are renting a property or working full time, if you are retired, if you are in a same-sex relationship, if you are single or if you have your own home. There is also a misconception that you must foster for the long term, when actually we need people who can step up into emergency care roles and respite, short‑term and restoration roles as well.

Our message is clear: If you have got room in your heart and your home, the New South Wales Government will support you every step of the way to change a child's life. Better support for foster carers is a fundamental part of our Government's landmark reforms to child protection. Our $1.2 billion investment in this year's budget—which was pretty much all about child protection—has allowed us to increase support for foster carers and increase the foster carer allowance for the first time in 20 years. That begins on 1 January, so there has never been a better time to become a foster carer. As we head towards Christmas, I wish everyone a safe and happy time with their loved ones and ask everyone to back our foster care campaign and urge their communities to consider becoming a foster carer this Christmas to change a child's life.

Mr DAVID HARRIS ( Wyong — Minister for Aboriginal Affairs and Treaty, Minister for Gaming and Racing, Minister for Veterans, Minister for Medical Research, and Minister for the Central Coast ) ( 12:19 :05 ): In line with Standing Order 131 (7), I provide additional information in relation to the question from the member for Balmain on the topic of gambling harm minimisation that I answered at 12:12 p.m. on Wednesday 22 October 2025. In my answer, I stated, as reflected on page 22 of the full-day Hansard PDF:

The panel concurred with Liquor and Gaming's finding that the six-hour shutdown period currently in place is effective at minimising gambling harm and should be maintained.

I will clarify. The panel considered Liquor and Gaming NSW's finding that the six-hour shutdown period currently in place is effective at minimising gambling harm, and the Roadmap for Gaming Reform report recommended that the six-hour shutdown period be maintained. The clarification makes clear that the Liquor and Gaming NSW review report was an input in the panel process and that the six-hour shutdown period was a recommendation in the final road map report.

tree_branches.text:
Debate resumed from an earlier hour.

I also acknowledge the work of parliamentary staff. They do a significant amount of work behind the scenes at all times and do that with patience. Sometimes I wonder how they do it. We can be fickle at times; we chop and we change. Even with events and things like that, they are able to accommodate changes and requests that other venues certainly would not; I speak from experience. A big thank you to the Clerks, the Legislative Assembly team, Hansard, committee services, the library, IT, corporate services, building and facilities, security, food and catering and, of course, the cleaners. It is always a sign that we are doing well when we see a smile or a giggle from Hansard sitting in the loft.

Mr Adam Crouch: Or a shake of the head.

Mr NATHAN HAGARTY: I do not get many shakes of the head. I say to them: Keep doing what you are doing. You do a fantastic job to make me sound like I can actually string a sentence together, so well done. Among the Chamber staff, I note the efforts of Peter, Nathan, David, Eve, Ainsley, Monica and Harriet, who deal with change, long hours and last-minute demands with good humour and dedication. I give special congratulations to a couple of people who have taken on new roles: Ian Delahunty, a long-time Chamber supervisor, who has stepped into the role of senior parliamentary officer for logistics and protocol; and Blake Russell, who is now Chamber supervisor.

A particular note of thanks from me goes to Gusti, my cleaner, who recently went on six weeks leave. She does a fantastic job and knows my particular quirks. When I come in every morning, everything is spick and span, so I thank her and will maybe speak to her boss about further holidays. I can use many adjectives, but I do not think I can fully describe her—the incomparable, irreplaceable Colleen. She handles the complexity of her job with aplomb. She does run the place. She makes me look good, which, I am sure my wife agrees, is a very difficult job. She does a fantastic job not just for Government members but also for Opposition and crossbench members.

Ms Sophie Cotsis: Hear, hear!

Mr NATHAN HAGARTY: Thank you. Recently, because of the House resolution of no quorums or divisions after 6.30 p.m., we thought we would trial a roster where the Deputy Whip, Colleen or I go home early. On each occasion when Colleen and I went home early, things have gone to the proverbial, so I think that is a sign of how well she can handle those situations. Let's be honest, we cannot thank her enough. I thank the Leader of the House, not just for his "Rontent" but also for the work that he does in the Chamber. I thank Omar for not just putting up with Ron but also the amazing work that he does in the office and for his guidance throughout the year.

I thank the leadership group and the Premier. Like other members who have spoken today, I send a message to the Deputy Premier. It was great to see her via video link this week. I cannot wait to have her back. The Deputy Whip only started recently and is doing a fantastic job. I think we make a fantastic team. Likewise, former Whip Janelle did a fantastic job. I know the Opposition Whip and I have our battles, but when we do the public service seminars, we turn into a fantastic team. I acknowledge his staff. We will most certainly miss Bo, and Anthony has big shoes to fill, but he is doing a fantastic job so far. Keep up the good work.

Back home in Leppington, which is one of the fastest growing communities, I thank everyone there and especially my staff: Sharon, Zeli and Neola. Sharon, my senior electorate officer, does a fantastic job. I cannot fathom some of the things that she deals with. I thank her for the way that she comes in day after day and gets through the amount of work she does. Neola came on this year. She is quite new and quite young but is also a real breath of fresh air. Zeli, who accompanies me to this place, does an amazing job. She does very long hours and puts up with some of my moods and demands during a long sitting day. A big happy birthday to Zeli. It is her birthday today, and I hope she is having a wonderful time.

I cannot forget the family. To my wife Christy and my kids Nia and Evan, you keep me grounded and you are my anchor. I certainly would not be doing this job without your support and tolerance. Watching them grow has been quite special. My daughter started university this year, so she is going very well. She has an exam today, so I wish her all the best. I will have a chat to her later about how that went. I give a special shout out to Cassidy from Kearns Public School. He is in year 4 and won my Christmas card competition. People across Leppington are eagerly waiting for that to slip into their letterbox. I have given thanks to everyone in Leppington, so I will leave it at that.

My good mate Richie Williamson, The Nationals Whip, is in the Chamber. Richie and I were talking today, saying that we make a great team. It is an absolute joy and pleasure to work with Rich. He is a wonderful person to work with. I also give a shout out to the Government Whip and the Deputy Government Whip, Liesl Tesch, who just entered the Chamber. I also give a shout out to Colleen Symington. Let's be clear: Colleen runs the place. Colleen, you are not allowed to go away or leave early, because every time you do, this place falls apart. I also acknowledge the incredible work done by the previous Whip's adviser, Bo Ok. She will be greatly missed. I look forward to catching up with Bo over Christmas. Welcome to Anthony Radic, who is doing a truly outstanding job with those big shoes to fill. It is a big job, and he is doing it incredibly well. Thanks, Anthony, for looking after all of us.

I also thank all of the team in here that do what they do every single day to make us look better, whether it be the incredible Hansard team behind me, the truly amazing Clerks in this place, led by the incredible Helen Minnican, with Carly and our Serjeant-at-Arms, Simon. I thank all of the Legislative Assembly attendants who keep this place running, including by putting the air conditioning temperature down at question time for me, because it gets very warm in here with 93 people all trying to talk at the same time. I often start a contribution by saying, "I will make a brief contribution", which means I will always go over time, but I will try and stay on message today.

I acknowledge all of my colleagues in the Opposition, both Liberals and Nationals, for the great work that they do for their electorates every single day, especially in this place—a lot of them travel a long way, like my friend Richie Williamson, and are away from their families for long periods—because we are proud and privileged to do what we do in this place. I acknowledge Gurmesh Singh, the new Leader of The Nationals, and the former Leader of The Nationals, Dugald Saunders. I acknowledge the whole leadership team in the Liberal Opposition. They do an incredible job.

I am really pleased that the member for Wyong is present in the Chamber. I thank him, too, for his friendship and camaraderie in what has been a pretty tough year and a half for me. I greatly respect the work that he does. I know how tough it is being in government. I will keep saying to him: "Be an irritant and go for every single dollar." He knows exactly what I mean by that. The member for Wyong is a great representative of the Central Coast—it is a pleasure working with him—as is the member for Gosford.

Mr David Harris: We share views on council.

Mr ADAM CROUCH: Absolutely. I have a deep sense of gratitude to the truly amazing people of the Terrigal electorate. It is a privilege and an honour to represent them and be the voice for our community in this Parliament. I thank them, as their elected representative, for the continued support they have provided me, and for their genuine caring, which means everything to me. They know what that means. Not a day goes by where someone does not ask how I am going. I am very privileged to have 55,000 support workers, and I am very lucky to represent them. They are a truly incredible group of people. It is an awesome responsibility and privilege, which I love doing, every single day.

I thank my incredible electoral office—Jack Robinson, Donna Golightly, Julie McFadden, Debra Beattie and Adam Walton—for doing the best job of looking after a wonderful group of people. I am so proud of what they do every single day. I boast that I have the best team anywhere. I know everyone says that, and we do. We are so lucky to have great electoral office staff who spend so much time caring for the people that we represent. Obviously they take their jobs very seriously. I hope they have a well-earned Christmas break. In general, I wish everybody here a very merry Christmas, and a safe, prosperous and happy holiday time. It is time to spend with family, to have a break and—for those of us from the Central Coast—appreciate that we live in the best region, in the best State, in the best country in the world. We are so lucky to be able to spend time in those electorates and at home with our family, our loved ones and our friends.

Ms Trish Doyle: Wrap it up.

Mr ADAM CROUCH: I hear the member for Blue Mountains. I have not gone anywhere near as far over my time as the member for Leppington did. I am also better dressed than him today. Again, I thank my electorate and the spectacular community of the Central Coast. Have a safe and merry Christmas. It would be remiss of me not to thank our incredible volunteer surf lifesavers for the 100,000-plus hours that they are going to put in on our beaches, keeping 1.2 million people safe again this season. They are true rockstars, and they do their job for free because they want to keep people safe. I thank the team at Surf Life Saving Central Coast and my seven Surf Life Saving clubs for all the hard work they are going to do this season. We know that they go out there to keep everybody safe. Again, I wish everyone a very merry, safe and happy Christmas.

We have seen huge changes in Gosford this year, with an exciting time coming up. I think the Premier is coming up to the coast in a few days to celebrate the opening of the fantastic Archibald building. The topping out has occurred. It is ready and it is operating: We have got a five‑star hotel on the Central Coast. To any members who are listening from their offices, we have got a new beautiful destination in the City of Gosford, five‑star service and gorgeous apartments there as well. We also have a new university—I have had a sneak peek, and the students are coming in a few days to have a look around—which will be operating next year as well.

My office has done an amazing job, with over 10,000 interactions with the local community this year, so I start by thanking our office team, and I will come back to them further down the track. Another amazing feat in 2025 has been LIGHT UP. The death of Audrey Griffin was a tragic time, but in true Central Coast spirit we have celebrated her life with an incredible concert in polytec Stadium. The event was a beautiful coming together of the community. It reflects the strength of the Central Coast community.

In felicitations, I thank our public servants. I know this year has been a very important year for our public service. As a former teacher, I thank our teachers and I wish them a very happy holiday. They really deserve it. I thank our hard-working nurses, our firies, our police and everyone who works on the train system. We met with Transport for NSW, who are working hard to improve the trains running on time across our community. We appreciate everyone working on the stations in my home electorate. I thank the people who work in the long service section up there on the Central Coast, SafeWork NSW, Invest Regional NSW, Destination NSW and all the other public servants who live and/or work on the Central Coast. We value you, we respect you, and we thank you for your service.

I also thank my beautiful Central Coast Labor team. The member for Wyong is present in the Chamber. I know the member for The Entrance in the building somewhere, as is the feisty member for Swansea. The four of us getting together on a regular basis to fight for the coast is a really important part of our wellbeing, as well as looking after our community. I also acknowledge the member for Terrigal, who is fighting hard for our community as well. I acknowledge the Premier and wish him a very happy Christmas break. I do hope he gets a rest. I thank him for his continued support of me in this role. I also thank my fantastic Minister, Kate Washington, and her team. It is an honour to work beside Kate, who is so passionate about family and community services, and disability inclusion.

I thank the fabulous parliamentary staff, and I see Hansard waving and smiling up there. We do have a laugh every now and then. I thank our fantastic Chamber attendants. It was lovely to see Dave's little baby in the Chamber today. I thank the facilities group, and the IT group, who I emailed this morning. They try to look after our IT in just seconds, which is amazing. I thank our cleaner, and I know my Whip mentioned Gusti, who does a great job looking after our offices. The library staff are some of my favourites. I like to visit them whenever I can.  And I know we all enjoy and appreciate the catering staff. The food we have here in Parliament is always exceptional. I also thank the special constables, who are there as we come to and from Parliament. Many thanks to everyone else who works here in this building.

I thank my beautiful friend, the Speaker, and his panel. He does an amazing job leading the panel. The Speaker's team are really important to us as well. Thank you, Madam Temporary Speaker. I thank the women in the New South Wales Parliament. The cross-party camaraderie of the women in this place is really important as we see the number of women grow in the Parliament. I thank and wish merry Christmas to my community groups. Every electorate has its Lions, Rotary, Country Women's Association and Probus. They do an amazing job in our community, looking after each other but also identifying things that need to happen in our community. I thank everyone in our night-time economy sector. Central Coast Music and Arts, the FunHaus Factory and everyone who works in that sector are so important. We are changing that sector as best we can.

The Central Coast Women's Health Centre, our homelessness interagency group, Coast Shelter, Pacific Link and Volunteering Central Coast all do an amazing job. Before I finish, I would like to tune in on my beautiful office team. Joely, my chief of staff, is having a happy holiday. Good on you, Joely. It is very well deserved. Jayden stepped into her shoes and does an amazing job. Han is in the office today, perhaps waving to us as I speak, and being so nice to our constituents. Erin joined the team this year, and she is so thorough and professional and such a positive delight to have in the team. So is Scott, who is so thorough and has such expertise at writing. The community often thinks I do the job, but my office staff really does all the work, and I just wheel out the front every now and then and wave to people. I have huge hugs for them and also for Kyra and Emily, who left our team this year. One is off to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions and one is off to the Federal Treasury, which is delightful.

The branchies in our Labor family on the Central Coast are so supportive and so important in my world. I thank the branch presidents and secretaries and all the volunteers, but also the branchies, for holding us to account and supporting our Labor values. It really is a joy. I thank our volunteer organisations—the RFS, the SES, the surf lifesaving clubs—and any other volunteers across our community. They are too numerous to name. May everyone have a fantastic, safe and happy Christmas, spend some time with loved ones, enjoy the summer and the beaches and, most of all, just be proud to call the Central Coast home.

I acknowledge the Premier and the work his Ministers are doing. But it is not lost on me that for much of this year we have been a member short. I have been thinking about the Deputy Premier, and I hope that her recovery is quick and we will see her back in 2026 on the front bench, next to the Premier. We will probably bowl her a couple of deliveries down the wicket, and I am sure that she will either let them go through to the keeper or have a crack at hitting them over the fence for six.

I acknowledge the great work that The Nationals, collectively, do here to hold the Government to account and represent the people of regional New South Wales. We do not carry that burden on our own; other members of this place also represent regional New South Wales. Every member who does the hard yards, leaving home at midday on Sunday to get to the city so that we can start our parliamentary week on a Monday and then sit on Tuesday, knows that it is a tough gig. I acknowledge the member for Dubbo, who for the past three years has led our party; our new leader, the member for Coffs Harbour; and our deputy leader, the member for Tamworth. I wish them all a happy and safe Christmas.

Of course, at this time we are thinking as well of the Clerks, the Hansard staff, the attendants and every other person who turns up here to help us to do our job of making New South Wales number one. My fellow Whips and I work pretty well as a team, I have to say. The text messages come through: "We're one short. We need a pair. Can we make this work?" We are pretty genuine in ensuring that indeed we do make the Parliament and the Chamber work as best we can. I think we have done that pretty well. I thank the Leader of the House and those on the Opposition benches for their counsel and advice. What people see in question time is probably not an accurate reflection of what goes on in this building. There are relationships across the divide. Truly, that is how this place works.

I thank my team at home—Debbie, Chris, Sarah, Mel and Jodi—for making me look good in the electorate. They do a tremendous job. I know that they will get some time off. I thank the Richmond and Clarence Valley mayors and councillors for the work they have done. Local government is important. I wish my Federal member, the member for Page, Kevin Hogan, and Karen all the best over the summer break. As I wrap up, I wish one and all in this building a genuine happy Christmas. They should relax and put their feet up. Collectively, we will be back in 2026 to continue the job of making New South Wales the very best it can be. Have a merry Christmas and a happy new year. I will see you in 2026. Ho, ho, ho!

Of course our kids and their families deserve the best, be it in education, health or entertainment, so I welcome the $200,000 special entertainment precinct trial now kicking off in Liverpool. It will help set our CBD on the path to becoming a vibrant university city with a large night-time workforce and help fulfil its potential. None of that progress would have happened without a government that was willing to listen. I thank our Premier, our Ministers and their staff members for their openness and readiness to engage with the issues that matter to Liverpool. I particularly send my best wishes to the Deputy Premier. It will be great to have her back in 2026.

I believe that being persistent is a core skill set of this job. Some might say that being called annoying is the highest compliment we can receive. Getting results for our communities often requires effective deployment of the vomit principle: When you are sick of repeating something, others might be starting to listen. I hope that I have been sufficiently annoying for everyone in the Ministers' offices this year. Members are only as successful as the support we have around us. At home in Liverpool, my staff is ably led by my fantastic senior electorate officer [SEO], Christy Nguy. It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good SEO makes our lives so much easier, and I am lucky to have the best. Besides her unwavering work ethic, which included answering emails after surgery, Christy's baked goods are highly sought after by members and others during sitting weeks. Here's hoping for more sweet treats and fewer flat tyres in 2026.

The team also includes our self-described office soundtrack, Liam Thorne, who provides us with daily entertainment whether we ask for it or not, as well as Mel Hadfield, who joined us this year and has taken to Team Livo like a duck to water. I thank them for enthusiastically joining the coffee, Aldi and Sydney Outlet Village runs. I give a special shout-out to the wonderful Hazel Neville. She has taken some time off this year, but I am happy to share that she will be back soon to join us for the holiday season and for a much brighter 2026. The office is not the same without her.
