tree_branches.name: Summary Offences Amendment (Police Memorial Offences) Bill 2025
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Bills > Summary Offences Amendment (Police Memorial Offences) Bill 2025
tree_branches.text:
That this bill be now read a second time.

I introduce the Summary Offences Amendment (Police Memorial Offences) Bill 2025. The intent of the bill is to extend the legal protection afforded to our war memorials to police memorials. In Australia we treasure and protect our sacred spaces. Our places of worship, significant historical sites and war memorials, for example, are all treated with particular reverence. There are things that a person might do in any other public place that they would not, and should not, do at those sacred sites. They are places where people gather with a common purpose to reflect on the past, to commemorate our forebears, to worship, to pay respects and to spend a moment in quiet contemplation.

While most people understand the importance of treating those spaces with reverence, there are some people who, for their own reasons, choose to show disrespect, to disturb the serenity and to deface those places that are so important to many people. People who defile or disrespect our sacred spaces should be punished and others who contemplate such an act should be deterred from doing so by the threat of punishment. There has recently been legislation passed to protect the war memorial in Sydney, as well as other war memorials across New South Wales, from being vandalised or treated with other forms of disrespect. It is now an offence to act offensively at, or destroy any part of, the Sydney war memorial. The legislation even prevents people riding bicycles or skateboards within those spaces. That is as it should be. People who served in the military put their lives on the line, signing a blank cheque for their country. The Sydney memorial is a place of national significance. It is also an offence to damage any other war memorial.

That protection should also be extended to police memorials. Police hold an equally important place in our society; they serve and protect the public every day. Most of us are likely to regularly encounter, engage with or even personally know someone in the police. But like military service, police also sign a blank cheque for their community, not really knowing what each day may hand them and occasionally paying the ultimate price: losing their life in the line of duty. Police memorials are places where officers, past and present, often hold events to commemorate their colleagues who died protecting our way of life. They are also where friends and relatives of police who have died pay their respects to loved ones who have passed away. They are places to which all society should show the proper respect due to those who died and, by extension, all the people who have ever donned the uniform and served the public. We need a clear message that all those who serve deserve respect for that service. There needs to be a line drawn on behalf of all who serve that their service is off limits in activist campaigns or politicking.

In practical terms, the bill defines what a police memorial is within the Summary Offences Act and, like similar legislation for war memorials, makes it an offence for a person to wilfully damage or deface these protected places. It also makes it an offence for a person to commit a nuisance or an offensive act in, on or in connection with a police memorial. As it stands, people can be prosecuted for damaging any public property, but this bill will make police memorials protected places on par with war memorials. This will allow a judge to rule that a person's damage or disrespect to the memorial is driven by motives beyond just mindless destruction of public property and could, or should, attract a higher penalty.

Disrespect can come in many forms. It can take the form of physical destruction of something deemed sacred, or it can come from acting inappropriately in a place where people gather for peace, quiet and contemplation. We have failed to recognise in law the sacred and protected nature of our police memorials. Police work to keep us safe and to keep order in places where disorder threatens. They lay their lives on the line. The least we can do is show them respect by protecting their memorials and maintaining the solemnity of those spaces.

Debate adjourned.

tree_branches.name: Road Transport Amendment (Medicinal Cannabis) Bill 2025
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Bills > Road Transport Amendment (Medicinal Cannabis) Bill 2025
tree_branches.text:
That this bill be now read a second time.

The Road Transport Amendment (Medicinal Cannabis) Bill 2025 will stop the criminalisation through driving laws of people who lawfully use cannabis as medicine. I am introducing this bill on behalf of a number of co‑sponsors, including myself; the member for Wagga Wagga; the member for Wollondilly; the member for Barwon; the member for Lake Macquarie; and the Hon. John Ruddick, MLC; the Hon. Jeremy Buckingham, MLC; and the Legalise Cannabis Party, to which I pay special tribute for their collaborative work on the bill. Hopefully, the Hon. Jeremy Buckingham will have carriage of the bill in the Legislative Council should it pass this House.

It is estimated that over 100,000 people in New South Wales have a script to use cannabis as medicine. Cannabis is prescribed and used for a range of health and mental health conditions, including multiple sclerosis, cancer, Crohn's disease, epilepsy, neuropathic pain and post-traumatic stress disorder. It is often prescribed when conventional treatments are ineffective or have intolerable side effects. I am one of those people. I lawfully use medicinal cannabis to help with sleep and anxiety. I was initially prescribed valium; however, it made me feel groggy. Medical cannabis helps to restore my sleep and my daytime functioning, and has been transformative to my wellbeing.

This reform is not about me. As the member for Sydney, I do not really need to drive much at all. This reform is for the people across New South Wales who every day have to choose between taking legal, prescribed medicine for pain management, sleep, anxiety and a number of other health reasons, and working or visiting a loved one. Leading drug law reform advocacy organisation Unharm has shared stories with me about the impact that the current laws are having on individuals across New South Wales. One person wrote:

For me, it meant losing independence just to stay legal. My carer had to drive me everywhere. I have stage 4 cancer but I am fit to drive. I'd rather use cannabis than the legal opioids I am forced to use so that I can drive.

Another person said:

For me, it meant losing work and independence just to stay legal. I suffer 24/7 chronic pain and inflammation from multiple autoimmune diseases. Cannabis is the ONLY prescription I've tried that helps bring the constant 7 out of 10 pain down to tolerable levels.

Another person shared:

For me, it has meant losing what little independence I had as a chronically ill person, who is also a full time carer for my two disabled children. I finally found treatment that works for my medical conditions, but this law has isolated me from being able to access the community, obtain medicines to treat urgent sickness, and even from being able to buy food as needed, because most public transport is not accessible to me at my address. My car has sat unused in my driveway for six months because it is illegal for me to drive it for weeks after the last time I used medicinal cannabis, which I require almost every day.

Another person said:

For me, it means an added stress when I consume THC at night to help me sleep and relax my mind and body after spine surgery. I work in aged care with some of our most vulnerable people in our communities. Me consuming THC at night doesn't make me impaired the next day, but it is present in our bodies for weeks and even months. People on other pharmaceutical medications are able to drive. So why aren't we?

Another person wrote:

For me, it meant losing my job and independence. I have two artificial discs in my neck and I take prescribed medicinal cannabis to manage neuropathic pain. I was driving my work issued ute back from a job when I was waved over by a highway patrol officer doing RDT. It was more than 48 hours since I used the medicine, but after being swabbed "non negative" I was given a 24 hour driving ban. The lab took almost four months to certify the result. I haven't worked a day since—I was not fired, just not given work. In the end I was not convicted or fined. I was given a 12 month bond and costs. But my job was gone. My family has suffered from my lack 4 of work, we've battled eviction for months, and my mental health is cratered.

Another person said:

For me, it means chronic poor sleep. Without medicinal cannabis, my ADHD brain has me awake for -30 seconds out of every three minutes, and totally unable to sleep before 1-2am. That doesn't make for a restful night's sleep. Medicinal cannabis was almost miraculous in its ability to allow me to sleep before midnight, and actually get enough rest. However, the law won't allow me to drive if I use it. Ironically enough, it allows me to drive in my chronically sleep -deprived state.

Finally, another person shard:

For me, I take medical cannabis for pain and sleep issues. Before cannabis my doctor used to prescribe opioids for my pain and sleeping pills for my sleep issues. These drugs are far more dangerous than cannabis yet it is not illegal to drive if these are in your system. Since changing to medical cannabis, it has helped my pain and I sleep right through the night. I do not drive while intoxicated but because my pain and sleep issues are now properly treated I am a much safer driver on the roads. Yet legally I am not allowed to drive. I am not a criminal.

Cannabis has been lawful medicine in Australia since 2016. The Therapeutic Goods Administration published clinical guidance, the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia provides education resources and there are a range of professional development programs for prescribing health practitioners. But our driving laws have not been updated to treat medicinal cannabis like any other prescription drug. Tetrahydrocannabinol, which can be a component in medicinal cannabis, is tested for in roadside drug tests and a penalty notice can be issued if any trace of THC is detected. The offence applies even if the THC was lawfully consumed in accordance with a prescription and the person was not driving under the influence.

A roadside drug test can detect the presence of THC for up to a month after it was last consumed, long after the side effects of THC have worn off—normally only a few hours after consumption. People who lawfully use cannabis as medicine are being penalised when they drive with huge fines and loss of licence. The impacts on their lives can be devastating, including being prevented from working, studying, caring and getting to appointments, in addition to the associated stigma. We are not talking about people who are driving under the influence of THC. Driving under the influence is a community safety risk that is captured by a separate offence under section 112 of the Road Transport Act 2013 for the "use or attempted use of a vehicle under the influence of alcohol or any other drug". The offence that people who lawfully use prescribed medicinal cannabis commit, if they drive purely with residual traces of THC in their system, is section 111 (1) which solely concerns driving with the presence of THC or another listed illicit drug in oral fluid, blood or urine. The offence was created because THC was once illicit, but it can now be prescribed as medicine and, like any other therapeutic drug, it can be both lawfully obtained and consumed and unlawfully obtained and consumed. THC must now be treated like any other prescription drug.

The law has perverse impact beyond criminalising people who lawfully use medicinal cannabis and preventing them from driving. People who get relief from cannabis for their conditions and need to drive for transportation are ceasing to use their medicine and changing to other prescription drugs that are less effective and/or have more side effects because those drugs are not captured by the offence. Those drugs include opioids and barbiturates, which are proven to impact driving. Medical practitioners who prescribe cannabis cannot talk to their patients about safe driving; they can only tell them that it is unlawful to drive with any trace of THC in their system. Essentially, this means telling patients they cannot lawfully drive for a month after use.

Both the Legislative Council Portfolio Committee No. 1 inquiry into the impact of the regulatory framework for cannabis in New South Wales and the 2024 NSW Drug Summit co-chairs' report recommended an end to offences that criminalise medicinal cannabis users. These recommendations came from listening to experts and people with lived experience. The Road Transport Amendment (Medicinal Cannabis) Bill 2025 will exclude people who consume cannabis in accordance with a lawful prescription from the offence for driving with the presence of THC in their system, provided they are not driving under the influence, and have not been found to be driving with the presence of other illicit substances.

In the first six months after assent of the bill, the exemption would operate as a defence in court to provide time to update police operating guidelines. After six months, a person will not be subject to a penalty notice if they provide a police officer with evidence that the THC was lawfully used, unless the police officer has a reasonable belief the person did not lawfully use the THC or was driving under the influence of THC. Similar provisions also change the Marine Safety Act 1998 for operating a marine vessel. Avoiding court by not issuing a penalty notice at the roadside when a person provides evidence that they consumed THC lawfully—for example, through a prescription—will avoid wasting valuable court time, legal fees for the affected person and temporary loss of licence for a person who may need to drive.

Indeed, Unions NSW has a position statement in support of this. They also suggest that the Service NSW app or a person's driver licence may be another way to provide evidence of a script for medicinal cannabis. Police are already checking prescriptions to determine whether to issue penalty notices for cannabis possession charges. Courts will have no additional insight over police to determine whether a person was driving under the influence. The bill will not compromise safety. No other country that permits THC as medicine has driving offences for residual traces of the substance, and we know that residual traces do not impact driving. Safety is compromised when a person drives under the influence of THC, and the bill does not touch offences for that.

Many people use medicinal cannabis to get relief from pain, insomnia, appetite loss, tremor and other symptoms that have limited their life for years, but driving laws mean they must choose between that relief and being able to get to work or appointments or to see loved ones. People who live in regional and rural areas are most affected because they do not have the same transport options as those of us in the city. Current laws have no safety basis. They only stigmatise people who happen to suffer from an ailment that can be alleviated with medicinal cannabis, a substance that is lawfully prescribed in line with Therapeutic Goods Administration scheduling.

We need to treat people who lawfully use cannabis as medicine fairly, with dignity and in line with how we treat people using other drugs as medicine. To conclude, I pay particular tribute to the Hon. Jeremy Buckingham, who joins us here today. I thank him and his staff member, Pete Foster, along with my staff member, Tammie Nardone. They have worked closely to get this robust legislation right and ready to be introduced, debated and, I hope, passed by this Parliament early next year. I commend the bill.

Debate adjourned.

TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Michael Kemp ): I shall now leave the chair. The House will resume at 2.30 p.m.

tree_branches.text: Mr NATHAN HAGARTY ( Leppington ) ( 16:20 :30 ): It was a privilege to attend RSL LifeCare's annual fundraising gala, the 2025 Poppy Ball, held aboard HMAS Canberra (III) at Garden Island. The night was more than a celebration; it was a tribute to over 110 years of service to veterans and their families. What began in 1911 with the opening of the veterans home on Bare Island has grown into one of the largest care providers in Australia, now supporting over 13,700 people across more than 80 locations in New South Wales, the Australian Capital Territory and Queensland. Today, RSL LifeCare's services extend far beyond aged care. Programs like Homes for Heroes and Veteran Services offer housing, mental health support and financial assistance, and help veterans transition back to civilian life. Just last year, they provided over 900 nights of accommodation for veterans facing homelessness and more than $120,000 in direct support. I thank RSL LifeCare and everyone involved in the organisation of this year's Poppy Ball.

tree_branches.text: Mrs WENDY TUCKERMAN ( Goulburn ) ( 16:21 :33 ): I recognise Gunning Station and Connect@Gunning Station. On 2 November festivities were in full swing to celebrate the historic and innovatory second birthday of Connect@Gunning Station and the Sesquicentenary of Gunning Railway Station. This was a time to reflect and take time to acknowledge the historical significance of Gunning Station and the amazing restoration work that has been undertaken to now house Connect@Gunning Station. Although it is listed on the New South Wales State Heritage Register, the Gunning Station restoration project has unequivocally launched the station into a new life cycle, becoming a venue for a range of arts and cultural events, performances, heritage displays, workshops and a variety of other activities promoting Gunning and the wider region. The significance for the local community is vast, providing a place to connect socially and restore vitality within the village. I congratulate the director, Rose Marin, and the entire team at Southern Tablelands Arts on this remarkable achievement and wish them all the very best for continuing success and longevity.

tree_branches.text: Ms LIZA BUTLER ( South Coast ) ( 16:22 :41 ): Congratulations to Mollymook Golf Club on being named Most Outstanding Club, Facility or Place to Play (Regional) at the inaugural Golf Australia National Awards for Excellence. This incredible national honour follows the club's success last year, when it was awarded Country Club of the Year at the NSW Golf Industry Awards. This national recognition highlights how Mollymook Golf Club continues to set the standard for excellence by combining first-class facilities, a passion for the sport and an unwavering commitment to innovation and community. The club has created an environment where members, visitors and the wider community can come together and enjoy everything the South Coast has to offer. Congratulations to the board, staff, members and volunteers on this outstanding achievement, which showcases everything that makes Mollymook Golf Club such a proud part of our community.

tree_branches.name: Ms LIZA BUTLER

tree_branches.name: Nelma Brooks
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Nelma Brooks
tree_branches.text: Mr PAUL TOOLE ( Bathurst ) ( 16:23 :33 ): I acknowledge Nelma Brooks, a stand-out lady who has given so much to the community she lives in. Throughout her life, Nelma has volunteered for a range of community organisations, touching the hearts of countless individuals. Nelma was a well-known face at the Salvation Army store, stocking shelves and conducting community outreach, and visiting nursing homes for singalongs and worship services with the residents. Nelma has been running the arthritis support group for 20 years, coordinating monthly meetings with guest speakers and support services. Nelma spent seven years coordinating court support at Bathurst Courthouse. She was a companion for those attending court, offering a cup of tea or looking after young children while families attended hearings. Nelma has been involved in Operation Christmas Child for over five years, making it a family tradition to pack gifts for less fortunate families and shipping them across the world. Nelma has opened the doors of her own home to the group Knit Happens so they could continue their work knitting essentials for nursing homes and children. Nelma truly is one of a kind and I thank her for her selfless volunteering. She is a very worthy recipient of this acknowledgement.

tree_branches.name: Mr PAUL TOOLE
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Nelma Brooks > Mr PAUL TOOLE

tree_branches.name: Kiama Ultra Challenge
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Kiama Ultra Challenge
tree_branches.text: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY ( Kiama ) ( 16:24 :00 ): I recognise the extraordinary Kiama Ultra Challenge held at Kiama Surf Club, which raised an incredible $22,000 for four vital charities. World Indoor Rowing Champion Nardia Guillaumier from NEG Photography rowed 100 kilometres on her machine, while her coach Alan Swan rode 200 kilometres on a stationary bike. Some 12 community teams joined them throughout the day, rowing their machines continually throughout Nardia's challenge—a true display of collective endurance and spirit. The event supported Breast Cancer Network Australia, Kiama Surf Life Saving Club, the Leukaemia Foundation and the Australian Amyloidosis Network. Each charity holds special meaning for Nardia and Alan, but Nardia's motivation was deeply personal—her father, Bill, passed away from cardiac amyloidosis in August 2024. This is a rare disease with no cure. The brilliant Matt King from Creative Kooks saved his 258th surfboard from landfill, everybody signed it and it raised a whopping $2,350 on the day.

tree_branches.name: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Kiama Ultra Challenge > Ms KATELIN McINERNEY

tree_branches.name: Warringah Masters Swimming Club
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Warringah Masters Swimming Club
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL REGAN ( Wakehurst ) ( 16:25 :42 ): They say age is only a number, but for a relay team from Warringah Masters Swimming Club their combined age of 281 is pretty impressive. In August, John De Vries, 67, Jorian Catzel, 77, Stuart Meares, 64, and Gordon Whyte, 73, smashed the 4 x 50 metres men's 280+ age group medley relay at the World Aquatics Masters Championships in Singapore, winning gold with a time of two minutes and 26 seconds. The foursome was part of a 20-strong delegation from Warringah Masters, the largest swimming club on the northern beaches. I give a special shout-out to Collaroy resident Gordon Whyte, who at 73 trains up to four times a week and is already training for the next Masters competition in Budapest in 2027. His favourite stroke is butterfly, and he came fifth in the world across 200 metres after winning gold in the 100 metres event in the Masters Nationals in May. Gordon is supported by his faithful and very proud cheer squad—Lee, Sarah, Greta, Lisa, Amy, the next generation, Jack, and the newest edition at only a few weeks old, Nora. Congratulations Gordon, on all fronts.

tree_branches.name: Mr MICHAEL REGAN

tree_branches.name: Granville Waratah Soccer Football Club
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Granville Waratah Soccer Football Club
tree_branches.text: Ms DONNA DAVIS ( Parramatta ) ( 16:26 :43 ): It was great to join players, coaches and families as they celebrated the success of the Granville Waratah Soccer Football Club at the 2025 trophy presentation day. With trophies and tributes for players across the age ranges, a strong sense of pride and achievement was in the air as families came together with picnic baskets, blankets and shade covers to enjoy the lively atmosphere. The event did not just focus on the trophies; it had the perfect carnival spirit, with free rides and entertainment for all ages. From the youngest MiniRoos to the more seasoned players, everyone was able to enjoy the fun and make lasting memories. It was a pleasure to present Dev Shah with the Coach of the Year Award for the undefeated under-13s Division 3 Grand Champions. What an amazing achievement. I say a big "Woo hoo!" to all the Granville Waratah Soccer Football Club players, coaches and volunteers. It is their community spirit that makes the club so special.

tree_branches.name: Ms DONNA DAVIS

tree_branches.name: Davidson Electorate Christmas Celebrations
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Davidson Electorate Christmas Celebrations
tree_branches.text: Mr MATT CROSS ( David son ) ( 16:27 :42 ): It is beginning to look a lot like Christmas in the Davidson electorate. I am very proud to update the House that the Davidson Christmas Card Competition has a winner. I congratulate Esther from Covenant Christian School in Belrose for a wonderful card, which was "Christmas in Australia"—we had Santa, the kangaroos and the wombats out in the red desert. It was really wonderful, so congratulations to Esther. I also give a big shout-out to the best Christmas lights in all of Sydney—possibly all of Australia—in Borgnis Street, Davidson. A big thank you to all the amazing residents for all of their lights, smoke machines and projections, food trucks—you name it. A special thanks to the Rotary Club of Belrose and the Davidson Rural Fire Brigade for all the work they do, in particular for inviting Santa to come out. I look forward to being on Borgnis Street this year. A very special thanks to all the residents for supporting Bear Cottage.

tree_branches.name: Quota Club Narooma
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Quota Club Narooma
tree_branches.text: Dr MICHAEL HOLLAND ( Bega ) ( 16:28 :45 ): I was honoured to attend the thirty-eighth installation program of the Quota Club Narooma board on Saturday 8 November at Club Narooma. I congratulate the new board members: Christine Chatillon, Theresa Aston and Carol Hodges. Quota Club Narooma is a non-profit organisation supporting the social wellbeing of local communities, particularly women, children, the deaf, hard of hearing and speech impaired. In 2024-25 over $24,000 was presented by the Quota Club to various community groups, including South East Women and Children's Services, Cobargo Public School, Central Tilba Public School, Bodalla Public School, Narooma Public School, Angel Flight, the Shepherd Centre, Moruya District Hospital Auxiliary, and Monty's Place Narooma, who were represented at the dinner. Money has been raised through fashion parades, meat raffles, street stalls and trivia nights. Members have volunteered with the Red Shield Appeal and visited our local residential aged-care facilities. The motto of quota is "We share". Quota Club Narooma truly lives up to its motto. Our community thanks them.

tree_branches.name: Dr MICHAEL HOLLAND

tree_branches.name: Grafton District Meals on Wheels
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Grafton District Meals on Wheels
tree_branches.text: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON ( Clarence ) ( 16:29 :41 ): This afternoon in Parliament, I acknowledge the outstanding work of Grafton District Meals on Wheels. On 22 November the service will turn 60 years old, which we celebrated last Friday. In 1965, when the service started, it had 37 clients. Now it has 337 clients, 10 staff members and 90 volunteers. I give a special shout-out to Eleanor, who has been volunteering for Meals on Wheels for a massive 51 years. It is quite incredible. Nowadays it serves up to 102,000 meals a year to some of our most vulnerable in the community. Sometimes the knock on the door is the only interaction the clients have with the outside world. I congratulate Grafton District Meals on Wheels on a fantastic 60 years.

tree_branches.name: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON

tree_branches.name: Viqarunnisa Alumni Australia
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Viqarunnisa Alumni Australia
tree_branches.text: Mr TRI VO ( Cabramatta ) ( 16:30 :42 ): On 9 November 2025 I had the honour of representing the Premier at Viqarunnisa Alumni Australia's grand reunion and charity event in Bonnyrigg. Viqarunnisa Alumni Australia is the first Bangladeshi alumni association that serves to reconnect and build a network of former students of Viqarunnisa Noon School and College currently living in Australia. The school was established in 1952 in Bangladesh, where it served as an educational institution that provided education for girls. Over the past 73 years, it has become one of the renowned educational institutions in Bangladesh. Since the association's establishment in March 2017, it has been committed to reuniting alumni of this distinguished school. Their contributions vary from supporting various charity organisations to empowering individuals, including alumni who require assistance. I thank Dr Suranjana Rahman, president of the organisation, for the invitation and congratulate the members on their dedication.

tree_branches.name: Mr TRI VO

tree_branches.name: Lirra Peters-Dennis
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Lirra Peters-Dennis
tree_branches.text: Mr ROY BUTLER ( Barwon ) ( 16:31 :45 ): Walgett local Lirra Peters-Dennis is an inspiring young woman whose strength, determination and leadership reflect the best of her community. Growing up in Walgett, she faced many challenges, including unstable schooling, limited resources and personal hardship. In 2022 she lost her home in a fire, while coping with loss, violence and school instability. Despite this, Lirra remained focused on her education. Her perseverance earned her the Connected Communities Scholarship in 2023 and election as school captain in 2025. Through Walanga Muru's Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander entry pathway, she gained early entry to study a Bachelor of Psychology degree at Macquarie University in 2026, becoming the first Walgett Community College High School student to attend university. Lirra's journey embodies resilience, hope and the power of community support, showing what young people in rural areas can achieve through courage and determination. I congratulate Lirra on her achievements so far and wish her all the best for her future studies.

tree_branches.name: Mr ROY BUTLER
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Lirra Peters-Dennis > Mr ROY BUTLER

tree_branches.name: Ahmad Chatah
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Ahmad Chatah
tree_branches.text: Ms KYLIE WILKINSON ( East Hills ) ( 16:32 :48 ): I congratulate Ahmad Chatah on his appointment to the NSW Youth Advisory Council, following an extensive recruitment process that saw applicants compete for only 12 positions. The Youth Advisory Council plays a crucial role in ensuring that the voices of young people are heard when decisions that will shape their future are made. Ahmad has valuable experience in this area, being part of multiple student voice and advisory committees. He is currently a board member for the Australian Council for Student Voice. Ahmed is also a talented sportsman and has been selected to represent New South Wales in the National Junior Wheelchair Championships and is doing impressive work with wheelchair basketball as a member of the child-safe committee for Wheelchair Sports NSW. I look forward to hearing about the incredible things he will do for young people in the East Hills community and across the State. I congratulate Ahmad again on all these amazing achievements.

tree_branches.name: Ms KYLIE WILKINSON

tree_branches.name: Epping Electorate Community Organisations
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Epping Electorate Community Organisations
tree_branches.text: Ms MONICA TUDEHOPE ( Eppi ng ) ( 16:33 :42 ): I ask the Parliament to join with me in acknowledging and thanking the many organisations across the Epping electorate bringing our community together this year to celebrate Christmas. Christmas is a special time of year, especially for people of the Christian faith. It is also a time for families and communities to gather and to share in the spirit that makes this such a special season. These opportunities do not arise on their own. They are made possible because dedicated volunteers, community groups and local organisations give their time and energy to create events that allow us to celebrate. This year a number of groups have taken on that responsibility, ensuring that residents across our suburbs can enjoy festive celebrations. I particularly thank Beecroft Rotary Club, Carlingford Rotary Club, Alive 90.5FM, All Saints Anglican Church in North Epping, LifeWay Lutheran Church and the Parramatta council for their efforts in putting on Christmas carols, markets and celebrations and for putting up Christmas trees around the community. In addition, there will many churches celebrating Christmas, and I thank them for their efforts. I wish Epping a merry Christmas.

tree_branches.name: Shayna Humanitarian Leadership Program
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Shayna Humanitarian Leadership Program
tree_branches.text: Dr DAVID SALIBA ( Fairfield ) ( 16:34 :44 ): I recognise the outstanding achievements of the graduates of the leadership program of Shayna Humanitarian Services, in partnership with Unbound Stories and the Institute for Economics and Peace. This year's program focused on building social cohesion and peace by empowering young emerging leaders to take on meaningful roles in their communities. Participants received internationally recognised training, collaborated with local services and developed projects that address antisocial behaviour and support access to education and employment. I commend the 23 graduates of this year's program for their dedication and commitment to making New South Wales better. I extend sincere thanks to all those who supported this initiative, including Oliver Slewa, Multicultural NSW, community leaders and representatives from the NSW Police Force and SBS. Their combined efforts continue to inspire and nurture leadership and harmony across our community.

tree_branches.name: Dr DAVID SALIBA

tree_branches.name: Tribute to Robyn Shanahan
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Tribute to Robyn Shanahan
tree_branches.text: Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN ( Northern Tablelands ) ( 16:35 :44 ): I recognise the life and service of Robyn Shanahan, an Armidale local and devoted member of Armidale City Band for over 60 years. Robyn joined the band in 1965, at the age of 10. In 1989 Robyn began playing the cornet, performing at commemorations for Anzac Day and other memorial services. From the 1980s Robyn held various leadership roles, notably creating history as the first female president of the band, in 1992. Robyn was named a life member of the band and awarded the Band Association of NSW's award of merit, and received a 50-year long-service badge. The band has applied for the 60-year pin in Robyn's honour, to present to the Shanahan family. Robyn gave back to her community in spades, volunteering with the band over six decades. Regional towns' community organisations like the Armidale City Band flourish because of volunteers like Robyn, giving their time and expertise to benefit others. I give my sincerest condolences to her family. Robyn will be deeply missed.

tree_branches.name: Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Tribute to Robyn Shanahan > Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN

tree_branches.name: Australian Islamic Cultural Centre
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Australian Islamic Cultural Centre
tree_branches.text: Ms CHARISHMA KALIYANDA ( Liverpool ) ( 16:36 :43 ): I recently had the pleasure of attending the open day hosted by the Australian Islamic Cultural Centre at Masjid Bilal—Bilal Mosque—in Hinchinbrook. This wonderful event created a welcoming space for people of all backgrounds from across the Liverpool community to visit the mosque, meet members of the local Muslim community and deepen their understanding of Islamic culture and traditions. Open days like this are vital in fostering mutual respect and strengthening community bonds. They highlight the important role that mosques play in our local area, not only as places of worship but also as hubs for learning, charity and connection. It was inspiring to see so many residents walk through the doors, engage in meaningful conversations and show genuine interest in the beliefs and practices of their neighbours. These moments of openness and curiosity make our community stronger and more inclusive. I extend my sincere thanks to the Australian Islamic Cultural Centre and the dedicated team at Masjid Bilal for their warm hospitality and for creating such an informative and welcoming day. Their efforts truly help bring our communities closer together.

tree_branches.name: Palestinian Christians In Australia Organisation
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Palestinian Christians In Australia Organisation
tree_branches.text: Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) ( 16:38 :44 ): The Palestinian Christians in Australia [PCIA] held its fourth annual gala dinner on Friday, which was a tremendous success, with attendance by community members and many parliamentary colleagues. I acknowledge the esteemed Palestinian journalist Samer Tarazi, who has recently arrived from Gaza, who shared his experience of sheltering in a church and a harrowing description of escaping death while reporting from one of Gaza's hospitals before it was flattened by the Israeli army. The highlight of the evening was the stunning fashion parade showcasing Palestinian embroidery or tatreez. For Palestinians, tatreez is more than just an art form; it is a living story that tells of the Palestinian struggle and resilience. The proceeds of the evening will go towards supporting 15 students in Palestine to enter university, demonstrating the community's enduring commitment to education. I especially thank Suzan Wahab, president of PCIA and her team for putting on an amazing event and for her leadership, hard work and dedication in serving the needs of Palestinians, both Christian and Muslim.

tree_branches.name: Ms JULIA FINN

tree_branches.name: Annalise Nguyen
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Annalise Nguyen
tree_branches.text: Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA ( Drummoyne ) ( 16:39 :43 ): I sincerely congratulate Annalise Nguyen from St Ambrose Primary School in Concord West, who is the winner of the 2025 Drummoyne Electorate Christmas Artwork Competition. The competition is a special tradition in our community, giving local students the chance to share their creativity and show us what Christmas means to them. This year's theme, "An Aussie Christmas", invited young people to reflect on the unique way we celebrate Christmas in Australia, and Annalise captured it beautifully. Her artwork radiated the warmth, colour and joy that we all associate with an Aussie Christmas. Her artwork will be featured on my Christmas card and in my community newsletter this year. I sincerely congratulate Annalise on her outstanding artwork, and I thank all of the students who took part in this year's competition. I thank to the many families, parents and teachers for dropping off the hundreds of beautiful artworks we received this year. They will all be on display in my electorate office and on its front windows throughout December. Once again, I congratulate Annalise from St Ambrose and wish her all the very best.

tree_branches.name: Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Annalise Nguyen > Ms STEPHANIE DI PASQUA

tree_branches.name: Glenworth Valley Wilderness Adventures
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Glenworth Valley Wilderness Adventures
tree_branches.text: Ms LIESL TESCH ( Gosford ) ( 16:40 :47 ): It is with some fanfare that I inform the House of the achievement of a Central Coast destination that was recently named among the world's best adventure getaways. Family-owned Glenworth Valley Wilderness Adventures, just 15 minutes west of Gosford and 60 minutes from the Sydney CBD, has been named one of the world's 10 best adventure holidays in the annual Traveller Awards. That puts Glenworth Valley in the same company as hiking Kilimanjaro, Georgia's Transcaucasian Trail and Argentina's Iguazu Falls, as ranked by Traveller , a publication of The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age . Anyone who has been to Glenworth Valley can vouch for the breathtaking natural location in the Central Coast hinterland and the action‑packed range of outdoor activities from horse and quad bike riding to kayaking and abseiling. The 3,000‑acre wilderness property also offers camping, glamping and eco-villa stays and was recognised for its unique blend of wilderness, adventure and immersive natural beauty. General manager Mia Lawler said it is an "incredible privilege to be placed among such a prestigious list of global adventure destinations". The esteemed recognition belongs to every staff member, guide and visitor involved.

tree_branches.name: Ms LIESL TESCH
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Glenworth Valley Wilderness Adventures > Ms LIESL TESCH

tree_branches.name: Guy Guiana
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Guy Guiana
tree_branches.text: Mr DAVID LAYZELL ( Upper Hunter ) ( 16:4 1 :54 ): Hunter Valley Police District has today farewelled Chief Inspector Guy Guiana, marking the completion of his 38-year career with the NSW Police Force. Chief Inspector Guiana trained at the Goulburn police academy in the late 1980s. His service in the NSW Police Force has included general duties, detective, anti-theft squad and police airwing crewman. His rise through the ranks saw Guy promoted to inspector, beginning more than 20 years of service in the Upper Hunter. Inspector Guiana was further promoted to the rank of chief inspector and decorated with an Australian Police Medal awarded in the Australia Day 2013 Honours List. Chief Inspector Guiana's final day of service has been acknowledged with a ceremonial farewell at Muswellbrook Police Station, where he was marched out to the sound of bagpipes. I thank Guy for his contribution to New South Wales and the communities of the Hunter Valley, particularly the Upper Hunter.

tree_branches.name: Mr DAVID LAYZELL
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Guy Guiana > Mr DAVID LAYZELL

tree_branches.name: Australian International Academy Strathfield Campus
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Australian International Academy Strathfield Campus
tree_branches.text: Mr JASON LI ( Stra thfield ) ( 16:42 :56 ): I recognise the Australian International Academy, Strathfield, for its school captain elections. The annual event reflects the school's commitment to student voice, civic responsibility and active participation in democratic life. The election process mirrored a formal New South Wales ballot this year, giving students valuable hands-on experience with voting procedures and reinforcing fairness and transparency in decision-making. I was pleased to attend part of the process and was impressed by the energy and interest shown by the student community. Their engagement reflects a strong culture that encourages leadership, representation and respectful participation. I congratulate all students who nominated. I say well done to Zahra Afzal for putting herself forward and congratulations to Mona Taleb, who was elected school captain and Manahil Amir, who was elected vice-captain. I wish them every success in the year ahead. The spirit shown by the students reminds us that democracy is strongest when young people are empowered to learn it, practise it and lead it.

tree_branches.name: Mr JASON LI
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Australian International Academy Strathfield Campus > Mr JASON LI

tree_branches.name: Tribute to John Hill
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Tribute to John Hill
tree_branches.text: Mr TIM JAMES ( Willoughby ) ( 16:43 :00 ): I acknowledge the passing of a great citizen of Willoughby Mr John Hill, who passed away peacefully on 23 October 2025. John established John Hill and Co in 1977, building the real estate firm on honesty, integrity and service. Over nearly five decades, he became a respected leader in property known for his deep knowledge, professionalism and genuine care for people. His guidance and mentorship shaped generations of agents and set enduring standards across the industry. John served as president of both the Real Estate Institute of New South Wales and the Real Estate Institute of Australia, where he championed ethics and professionalism. He also held many other leadership roles, including chair of Real Cover Insurance, and contributed to advisory committees for government and industry bodies. Beyond business, John supported many community causes, including the Red Cross, hospitals and, indeed, the Liberal Party. John is remembered as a leader, mentor and friend whose legacy continues through his family, colleagues and the firm he built. I extend my sincere condolences to his wife, Virginia, son, Sam, daughter-in-law, Nicola, and his three grandchildren. Vale, John Hill.

tree_branches.name: Mr TIM JAMES
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Tribute to John Hill > Mr TIM JAMES

tree_branches.name: Pink Up Berry
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Pink Up Berry
tree_branches.text: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY ( Kiama ) ( 16:44 :00 ): I recognise the extraordinary Pink Up Berry campaign, which raised an incredible $108,000 and counting for the McGrath Foundation, surpassing last year's total. From 77 volunteers knitting year round to wrap trees in pink, to local businesses and residents decorating their homes and shopfronts, everyone plays a part in turning the town pink each October. The fundraiser included trivia nights, raffles, stalls, a race day held by Shoalhaven Turf Club and a beautiful luncheon with venue and staffing donated by The Homestead and catering donated by Garnish Creative Catering. I commend the Pink Up Berry committee, Deb Woolford, Kerry Carter, Pauline Windley, Sandy Bramley and Karen Brooks, for their tireless dedication. I congratulate the best decorated businesses, the Rutledge Bar and Eats, Dr Chambers at Berry Family Medical Practice and NSW Mobile Travel Agents, who also raised $22,000 for the cause. Well done to everyone.

tree_branches.name: Ms KATELIN McINERNEY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Pink Up Berry > Ms KATELIN McINERNEY

tree_branches.name: Lions Club Port Macquarie Tacking Point
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Lions Club Port Macquarie Tacking Point
tree_branches.text: Mr ROBERT DWYER ( Port Macquarie ) ( 16:45 :00 ): I acknowledge members of the Lions Club of Port Macquarie Tacking Point, who embody the spirit of service and compassion that strengthens our community. Through initiatives such as the Breakfast Club, disaster relief efforts and support for local schools and charities, the club has made a lasting impact on countless lives. Central to those efforts is club president Max Carrick, whose leadership and commitment to volunteerism drive the club's success, along with massive support from every one of the 37 club members. One key program is the Breakfast Club operating at Hastings Secondary College campuses to provide nutritious breakfasts for students. A new kitchenette at the Westport campus is planned to further support the initiative. I also recognise Gordon Cooper, who leads the Lions Eye Health Program, a vision screening and education initiative for early detection of eye health issues in children. The club's work not only meets immediate community needs but also fosters a culture of generosity and responsibility. I honour the club and its remarkable volunteers for their unwavering dedication to service and for enriching the lives of those in our electorate.

tree_branches.name: Mr ROBERT DWYER
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > Lions Club Port Macquarie Tacking Point > Mr ROBERT DWYER

tree_branches.name: St Raymond's Maronite Parish Auburn
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Community Recognition Statements > St Raymond's Maronite Parish Auburn
tree_branches.text: Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) ( 16:46 :00 ): I was delighted to join the congregation of St Raymond's Maronite church in Auburn on Sunday for their feast week mass and lunch at the family fun day—the feast day of St Raymond being on Tuesday 18 November. Bishop Antoine Charbel Tarabay conducted the mass along with Father Charbel Abboud and Father Charbel Dib. Many of the congregation are from the village of Hadchit in Lebanon, and St Raymond's in Auburn is named after the church in Hadchit and the patron saint of the village, St Raymond. Also known as Romanus of Caesarea, St Raymond was a fourth century martyred deacon who was killed during Emperor Diocletian's persecution of Christians. St Raymond's is one of the fastest growing Maronite parishes in Australia, and the congregation on Sunday was huge. I wish a happy feast day to St Raymond's parish and everyone named after St Raymond.

tree_branches.name: Wahroonga Electorate Community Building Partnership Grants
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Wahroonga Electorate Community Building Partnership Grants
tree_branches.text:
At PCYC Hornsby-Ku-ring-gai, a grant of $18,000 will provide new gym equipment, including a pendulum squat machine and SkiErg. The upgrade benefits gym members, local sporting teams, school sport programs and police initiatives, and helps young people build strength and confidence while engaging in activities that promote wellbeing, whether at the Mark Taylor Oval in Waitara or elsewhere. Education is a cornerstone of our community, and several schools have received vital support in this round of grants. The Wahroonga Public School's P&C Association received $100,000 to resurface sports courts and cricket nets. That will create multi‑sport spaces for students and the wider community after the public school had not received a Community Building Partnership grant for some years. The Normanhurst Public School's P&C Association received $25,000 to continue its sensory garden project, which will transform unused space into an inclusive outdoor learning environment.

The Pymble Public School's P&C Association received $30,000 to upgrade play equipment for students in years 3 to 6, which will create a safe and engaging space for over 300 students every day. The Pennant Hills High School's P&C Association received $38,657 for shaded seating areas, which will give students comfortable spaces to learn and socialise outdoors. That is incredibly important to the school's outdoor learning areas. The Normanhurst Boys High School's P&C Association received $10,000 to upgrade its canteen furniture, which will improve wellbeing and interaction for students and volunteers.

Sporting organisations are also benefiting from this round of grants. The Kissing Point Sports Club received $7,014 to upgrade coaching equipment and introduce a uniform hire program to encourage participation in netball. It also received $15,000 for audiovisual equipment to enhance the clubhouse experience for members and volunteers. The Kissing Point Sports Club is one of the largest sporting clubs in my electorate. Meanwhile, Thornleigh Sports Club—another big multi-sports club in the electorate—received $12,540 to restore the cricket pitch and surrounding areas at Thornleigh Oval, which will ensure safe and playable grounds for local competitions. That has been an issue for some years because of bad weather.

Community safety and wellbeing remain priorities for the allocation of funding. The 2nd Turramurra Scout Group received $27,817 to replace deteriorated hall eaves and fascia boards, remove hazardous asbestos and install a defibrillator. They are critical improvements that will protect health and extend the life of that important facility, which is completely maintained by volunteers and grants of this kind. Streetwork Australia Limited received $12,735 to upgrade iPads for youth caseworkers to enable better delivery of programs that support vulnerable young people. Lifeline Harbour to Hawkesbury Sydney received $33,916 to replace its van, which will ensure the continued collection and delivery of pre-loved goods that fund life-saving mental health services.

Faith and cultural organisations have not been forgotten. The Danish Church in Australia received $10,000 to create a covered outdoor area, which will offer a safe and welcoming space for children and community members to gather. Similarly, Thornleigh Community Baptist Church received $61,456 to refurbish its auditorium and adjoining office, which will improve facilities that serve a wide range of community groups. Some of our youngest learners will benefit from this round of grants too. Uniting Preschool Turramurra - TurraTots received $20,000 to resurface its verandah play area, which will enhance safety and comfort for children during active play and learning.

Finally, we are supporting emerging sports. The Sydney Northern Rays Water Polo Club received $27,865 to acquire a timing board and scoreboard. That will help the growing club provide better experiences for players and spectators. Those projects demonstrate the importance of governments investing in local communities. Unfortunately, the Minns Labor Government has not made any significant investments in my local community.

tree_branches.name: Grace Kennedy
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Grace Kennedy
tree_branches.text:
The International Surfing Association has worked closely with the International Paralympic Committee to refine classification systems and ensure that athletes are recognised for their skill, courage and performance, and not defined by their disability. Through those efforts, para surfing has built a clear pathway for athletes to train, compete and represent their nations at the highest level. The sport builds resilience, confidence and community values that mirror the very best of the Paralympic movement. At its heart, disabled surfing plays a vital role in fostering social inclusion. Across the South Coast—and, indeed, across Australia—we see volunteers, coaches and clubs opening the doors of our beaches to everyone. Organisations such as the Disabled Surfers Association and community-led initiatives make it possible for people of all ages and abilities to experience the freedom of the ocean.

The beach has long been part of our Australian identity. It is a place where barriers fall away, where laughter is shared and where community thrives. Through surfing, we see friendships formed, confidence restored and people rediscovering their sense of purpose. It is inclusion in its purest form, and it is achieved not through policy or theory but through compassion, connection and courage. With the assistance of people such as Grace and James Gissing from Good Surf, I want to see para surfing become part of everyday boardriding clubs throughout New South Wales. I am putting Ulladulla Boardriders on notice. I am coming their way very soon to begin this important initiative. Including para surfing in the Paralympic Games would be a natural and powerful next step. The sport already meets the standards of international competition, classification and governance. More importantly, it embodies the Paralympic values of determination, equality and inspiration.

Grace Kennedy's success is living proof that our para surfers are ready. Grace's bronze medal on the world stage shows not only her exceptional talent but also the strength of Australian coaches like James Gissing, our volunteers and our community spirit that supports athletes from the shoreline to the world arena. By welcoming para surfing into the Paralympics, we would give recognition to thousands of athletes who have trained tirelessly, often without funding or fanfare, to demonstrate what true resilience looks like. We would affirm, on a global stage, that sport belongs to everyone.

Grace Kennedy's journey reminds us that the ocean belongs to all of us; it does not see ability or disability, only determination and spirit. Grace's achievement inspires every young person watching from our South Coast beaches and every person with a disability who dreams of feeling the spray of the ocean on their face. It is time that para surfing, a sport that so perfectly captures Australia's love of the ocean and our belief in inclusion, is recognised on the world's greatest stage, the Paralympic Games. I congratulate Grace, and every para surfer blazing a trail for equality and recognition. They have not only made their community proud, but they have made a powerful case for a more inclusive future in sport, and in life.

tree_branches.name: Renewable Energy
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Renewable Energy
tree_branches.text:
The entire plan is based on hope that transmission will magically appear on time, hope that the batteries will be built someday, and hope that the wind will always blow and the sun will always shine. Hope is not an energy policy. Meanwhile, regional New South Wales is being carved up like it does not matter. Prime farmland is being bulldozed for solar factories. Wind turbines taller than skyscrapers—as tall as 300 metres in some cases—are being dumped next to family homes. Transmission lines are cutting straight through communities, without proper consultation or compensation. Locals are being inconvenienced. They are being promised jobs and benefits, but there is very little of that in many communities.

The rollout is a farce because it is being driven by ideology. People are drawing on whiteboards and turning up in hard hats for photo opportunities, but the Government is far more interested in looking green than actually delivering power that works. The truth is simple: We need to make sure that we have proper energy supply in the State, but that should not be at the expense of regional communities. We certainly cannot expect regional communities to take all the pain just so the Government can tick a box. The Government needs to get real, with proper planning, proven technology and proper community consultation. New South Wales is being marched towards an energy disaster of the Government's own making. That current pathway is reckless and chaotic. The people of New South Wales deserve better.

The reckless renewable rollout is not only affecting the regions. We hear from those in the city that regional areas who do not want it are nimbys. Regional communities are bearing the brunt of the entire renewable rollout. It is no wonder metro MPs do not care. Before the last election, only 18 carefully considered renewable energy projects were approved. In the past 2½ years alone, over 60 have been approved and many more are racing to get into the pipeline. Each project proposed is getting the rubber stamp of approval before the ink dries on the proposal. The Government's agenda is clear. This week the public interest debate was about renewable energy. We heard comments from the Premier that they are not going to slow it down. They are going to continue to fast‑track renewable projects in regional communities.

Regional communities are being disadvantaged by the rollout of the projects. The Government needs to make sure that our communities are heard. Members in this place are making decisions on behalf of communities that they have not even met with or listened to. Ministers have not even bothered to front up to community meetings, or spoken to those people who will be impacted to see how their lives will be turned upside down. Local councils are moving motions at local government conferences. Renewable energy projects are being forced on our communities, and people are sick and tired of it. Our farmers have been working the land, our small towns have been held together, and our communities want to continue to work in those areas. The people feel that the impact of the projects do not allow them and their voices to be heard.

tree_branches.name: Westmead Institute for Medical Research
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Westmead Institute for Medical Research
tree_branches.text:
For over two decades, WIMR has been at the forefront of scientific discovery, driving clinical innovation and delivering translational research that changes lives. Its researchers are tackling some of the most urgent health challenges of our time, from cancer, infectious diseases and neurological disorders to diabetes, liver disease and cardiovascular conditions. What sets WIMR apart is not only the scale and quality of its research but its unwavering commitment to improving human health both in Australia and globally. Its work is recognised internationally and is a source of immense pride for our local community in Parramatta.

I recently had the opportunity to visit Phage Australia, based at WIMR, and was truly inspired by the remarkable work taking place inside those laboratories. Phage Australia is leading the charge in phage therapy, an exciting and rapidly developing area of medicine that offers a targeted alternative to antibiotics. That is especially important in the face of growing antimicrobial resistance, which is one of the most serious public health threats of our time.

A significant milestone has been the establishment of Australia's first phage biomanufacturing facility, backed by the New South Wales Government. The state-of-the-art facility enables the clinical translation and scalable production of phage-based therapies—a critical step forward for Australian medical research and treatment capabilities. During my visit, I met with Professor Jon Iredell, Director of Phage Australia, and heard compelling stories of patients whose lives have been transformed by the therapy. One young person, facing the terrifying prospect of amputation, made a full recovery thanks to phage treatment. These are not just medical breakthroughs; they are stories of hope, resilience and lives being changed for the better.

The phage biomanufacturing facility has provided access to life- and limb-saving phage therapy for patients around Australia through a $3.5 million New South Wales Government investment in 2023. I thank Minister Harris for his ongoing support for all that Phage Australia is doing in this groundbreaking field of medicine. I know that, on the day he made the current funding announcement, he met with Professor Iredell, along with researchers from the United States, the United Kingdom and South Korea who were visiting to learn from that world‑leading research program.

The program is also a powerful reminder of the life-saving innovation happening in Western Sydney. Often we walk past those buildings without knowing the incredible work underway inside—research and development that has the potential to change the future of medicine not only in New South Wales and Australia but also around the world. Australia is globally respected for the quality of our medical research, and institutions like WIMR are a shining example of that strength. They do not just advance science; they build partnerships, train future leaders and address health inequities in our communities.

One of the most impressive aspects of my visit to Phage was the women working in that place. It was inspiring to see the role that they were playing in that incredibly important world-leading research and to hear the stories of where they started and where they have come to. I thank everyone at the Westmead Institute for Medical Research, especially Executive Director Professor Phillip O'Connell. Their work saves lives, brings hope and showcases the very best of Australian research, innovation, science and compassion, and our potential to lead the world in manufacturing. I commend the achievements of WIMR and reaffirm my strong support for its continued success and future impact.

tree_branches.name: Artificial Intelligence
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Artificial Intelligence
tree_branches.text:
One of the key concerns raised during the workshop was the increasing use of AI in cybersecurity and defence. AI is not only being used by democratic governments; it is also being used by malicious actors to automate cyber attacks, spread ransomware and exploit vulnerabilities at a scale we have never seen before. Bad actors, whether they are state‑based or criminal organisations, are using AI to conduct sophisticated phishing attacks, generate malicious code and disrupt critical infrastructure. The rapid pace of technological development means that, if we as legislators are not proactive, we will fall behind those who seek to do harm.

AI is being used to generate disinformation to distort the political process through fear and reputational harm using deepfakes and synthetic media. Women, minority groups and community leaders are often targeted and public trust is being undermined. Existing State and national laws are not keeping pace with emerging threats and there are few useful laws elsewhere that we can adopt. We need to modernise laws to prevent the misuse of AI, including preventing harmful AI‑generated content, strengthening regulatory bodies and ensuring tech companies are held accountable for the spread of misinformation on their platforms. But regulation alone will not safeguard democracy. We must invest in digital literacy so that people have the tools and knowledge to navigate the emerging digital environment safely. Firewalls and encryption are not enough; people need to understand the threats and uses of AI.

Artificial intelligence can further entrench digital colonialism. Digital colonialism is the concept where technology helps to subjugate already vulnerable communities through the extraction of data without fair return, through environmental impacts on low-income communities and through the concentration of power and decisions in the wealthy few. Australia and New South Wales have a role to play in challenging that imbalance by promoting fairness, transparency and respect for digital sovereignty and by monitoring the impacts of technological progress on human rights, equity and the environment. We can partner with like‑minded democratic nations to work through the challenges together.

Collaboration will be essential as AI governance cannot be approached in isolation. Technology crosses boundaries, with most cybersecurity threats coming from overseas agents. We should continue to engage actively in international forums, sharing best practices, supporting regional partners and advocating for strong, enforceable standards that balance innovation with accountability. Artificial intelligence provides significant opportunities to advance our economy, health care and governance, and to help us find solutions to challenges like climate change. But we have a responsibility at all levels of government to ensure that it is not used for harm. I call on the Government to work towards laws that promote safe AI use that does not undermine democracy and safety and that prioritises people over profits and big tech.

tree_branches.name: Assyrian Australian Community
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Assyrian Australian Community
tree_branches.text:
As the State member for Prospect, I have been fortunate to meet many remarkable multicultural organisations across our diverse Western Sydney community. Each of them plays an integral role, caring for individuals and maintaining and promoting culture. As their representative in Parliament, I have been proud to stand before this House to share their rich culture and help advocate for their communities. The Sydney chapter of the Assyrian Democratic Movement [ADM]—or Zowaa—is a leading example. Based in the Prospect electorate, the ADM is an active social and political organisation whose members strive to preserve and protect Assyrian culture. Their advocacy efforts strengthen our Assyrian‑Australian community in Western Sydney and in their traditional homelands, including the Nineveh Plains and the city of Mosul.

Recently I was pleased to meet with a delegation from the ADM's political bureau in Iraq, Ninab Yousif Toma and Ashur Slewa Nico. I thank Immanuel Sada and George Adam from the ADM Sydney chapter for introducing me to those great individuals. During our discussion, I was moved to hear of the ADM's fight for the democratic rights of its communities. For over four decades, its members have fought, through prison, persecution and martyrdom, for an Iraq that honours all its peoples without distinction. To this day, they are still fighting and advocating for national partnership. The ADM's story is etched with tragedy: the massacre at Simele in 1933, the destruction of Sorya in 1969, the terrors of the Ba'athist years and the darkness of ISIS. Yet through every storm, its members have persisted. Each epoch tested their endurance, but their advocacy remained steadfast and peaceful, born from spiritual strength and an abiding love for their homeland.

Today the ADM—in Western Sydney and at their bureau in Iraq—calls for partnership. The movement calls upon Iraq to fulfil the promise of its own constitution: to uphold Article 125 of the constitution, guaranteeing cultural, linguistic, and political rights; to amend laws that allow the forced Islamisation of minors; to reform the quota system that silences smaller voices; and to acknowledge, at last, the Chaldean‑Syriac‑Assyrian people as the original inhabitants of Iraq. The ADM requests that on 1 April the Babylonian and Assyrian New Year be designated a national holiday. Above all, the people seek to live alongside their compatriots in peace, with their minority rights respected and contributing, as they always have, to the progress and unity of Iraq. In a century that has too often forgotten the lessons of coexistence, the ADM's vision of partnership is a balm to the politics of division. It sends a clear message that diversity is not a threat; it is, in fact, a foundation.

The Assyrian Australian diaspora is strengthening the social, cultural and economic fabric of New South Wales. In suburbs like Smithfield, Fairfield, Wetherill Park, Prairiewood, Wakeley, Edensor Park and Bossley Park, our Assyrian community has built its roots, with churches like St Mary's Assyrian Church of the East and St Thomas The Apostle Chaldean Diocese to schools like St Narsai Assyrian Christian College and St Hurmizd Primary School. Our Assyrian Australian community are preserving their language, culture and faith whilst embracing the values, traditions and democratic freedoms of Australia. They are living proof that diversity, when respected, is a foundation for strength. This attests to their call for representation and parity in Iraq, calls which are echoed across the Prospect electorate. I am proud to stand in support of our Assyrian Australian community in the hope that one day their people will live freely and securely as respected owners of and equals in their ancestral homelands.

tree_branches.name: Clarence Electorate
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Clarence Electorate
tree_branches.text:
A little further up the mighty Clarence River, a new civic hall is being built at Maclean, which will be incredible for the area. It will include a 290-seat auditorium, a function room, a modern stage and backstage area, a cafe-style food and beverage outlet, and dedicated car parking. Of course, all these amenities will be fully accessible. This was also made possible by funding from the previous Government, with the council also contributing some funds. The $10 million Yamba Road betterment project is still under construction, which was funded by the former Government following the 2022 floods. This is a great project because it lifts the height of Yamba Road, ensuring it will remain open for longer during flooding. I welcome this week's announcement by the Federal Government of funding for a similar project on Iluka Road at the Esk River. Lastly, the remarkable new Clarence Regional Aquatic Centre has been open for a few months, attracting 70,000 visitors over the winter months, which is quite remarkable. Thanks to funding from the Federal Government, a brand-new water slide will open in the coming weeks. I think there are actually two slides there. One is 75 metres in length and the other is 85 metres in length.

Mr Steve Whan: I hope you're the first one on it.

Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON: That reminds me of an episode of The Simpsons , when Homer got stuck in a water slide. So no, I will not be the first one on it, Steve. But others will be lined up to get on. I know the entire Clarence community will treasure this new centre. Like every electorate, Clarence has had its ups and downs. Temporary Speaker Barr, you have been in the chair a number of times when I have mentioned the biosecurity issue of white spot in prawns. Sadly, but respectfully, I have to say that the Government has dropped the ball. The current white spot biosecurity order will end on 9 December, yet the Minister has given fishing families no plan for getting back to work. They have no idea what will happen on 10 December. I urge the Minister to speak with fishing families in the Clarence community to outline the Government's plan.

Tragically, I report to the House that in the past 12 weeks the Clarence Valley has seen three alleged murders that have rocked the community. The police are doing a terrific job, but my electorate has seen a serious spike in crime. I will work with the Government, the police, the community—anybody—to ensure that those statistics go down. Despite its size, Clarence is not a highly populated electorate, so to see three alleged murders in the past few months is uncharacteristic. That was the second and final instalment of Richie's year in review. I thank the House.

tree_branches.name: Kiama Electorate Fundraising Events
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Kiama Electorate Fundraising Events
tree_branches.text:
I give a shout-out to the winners of Pink Up Berry's residents of the year prize. This year the town has already raised an outstanding $108,000. I also gave a community recognition statement about the Kiama Ultra Challenge. This gruelling endurance rowing event brought together 12 teams to back up the wonderful Nardia to row for the entire day. Not a single moment was missed, as local athletes showcased their determination and resilience. Some non‑athletes also took to the seat to take part and keep up with local heroes to raise much-needed funds for four different charities.

I recognise Homestead of Hope, which this year held a beautiful Melbourne Cup luncheon to raise funds to provide free meals, emergency accommodation and friendship in the wider community. Lastly, on Saturday, the fabulous Bondi2Berry Ride for Dementia Australia notched up its remarkable tenth year. The ride has become a cornerstone community event that combines a physical challenge with meaningful purpose. Cyclists rode 155 kilometres from Bondi to Berry along the State's scenic coastline, taking in the beautiful views, to raise crucial funds and awareness for dementia research and support services. This year the almost 200 participants raised more than $110,000 for dementia research. They knocked it out of the park. Locals turned out in droves at the Pit Stop in Kiama to welcome the riders and then again to celebrate them finishing in the town of Berry.

I congratulate Nick Young and the organising committee on this fabulous event. I thank the generous sponsors of those community events—businesses that dig deep into their pockets to ensure that funds are raised and community events are supported. I give a shout-out to them. It is week 44 of the Sunday Community Support Group, which gathers in Nowra every Sunday to hand out donations of food, clothing and toiletries. They will do that right through to the end of the year. I give a big shout-out to Kerry Fahey of Kerry's Klothes Kiama, Margie Tweedie at Care Essentials, IGA Berry and everybody else who generously donates to that group every week.

No round-up of our electorate's brilliant community spirit would be complete without the i98FM Illawarra Convoy. Now in its twenty-first year, the convoy delivered an absolutely triumphant result. It raised an incredible total of $2.3 million. That is just a fraction of the $30 million that the Illawarra Convoy has raised over the past two decades. It is an incredible event where a convoy of trucks, motorbikes and cars gather at the top end of our electorate and then over a few hours drive the back way down to Shellharbour Airport, where they marshal for a family fun day. More importantly, businesses compete every year to raise the most funds and be the lead truck. This year Ross Transport led the convoy, because they raised $305,000. More incredibly, thousands of people set up their camp chairs and eskies all the way down the route to cheer on the incredible convoy. I cannot wait for next year. I congratulate every single person in the electorate who donated, showed up or helped to organise that display of community spirit. I feel incredibly privileged to be representing our community in this place.
