TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Clayton Barr ): Merry Christmas to you too.

Ms ROBYN PRESTON: I speak about several momentous occasions that occurred recently within the Hawkesbury electorate. Known for its proud heritage and encompassing historic towns such as Windsor, St Albans, Richmond, Ebenezer and Wilberforce—to name a few—Hawkesbury is a special place to live in, visit and learn about. I am privileged to be the member for the electorate, and I thoroughly enjoy occasions when we reach and celebrate significant anniversaries and milestones in our community. This week the restored Thomas James Bridge was officially opened, and the event was an example of that great public pride and celebration. Located on Settlers Road at Wisemans Ferry, the bridge has played a crucial role in connecting regions of the Hawkesbury since its construction in 1830. The Thomas James Bridge holds the prestigious title of the oldest in‑use bridge on mainland Australia—a source of great pride for Hawkesbury communities.

Unfortunately, recent flooding severely compromised the area around the bridge, resulting in major landslips and impacting the safe use of the bridge for residents. Funding from the State and Federal governments' recovery program enabled reconstruction of the bridge, with local contractor Delaney Civil appointed to complete the project. I note that the member for Gosford is in the Chamber. She participated in the conversations that followed the tragedy on our shared boundary, as both councils reached out to us for support. Stages of preliminary site assessment, bridge reconstruction and adjacent rock face stabilisation were critical steps in achieving restoration of the site.

Admirably, huge efforts were made during the repairs. The 181 original sandstone blocks, quarried from the surrounding hillside in 1830 to build the bridge, were carefully removed from the site. The beautiful sandstone blocks, originally cut and moved by hand, were meticulously replaced in exactly the same position to honour and replicate the original bridge as much as possible. It is remarkable that it could be mirrored 195 years later. I was incredibly honoured to attend the reopening of the Thomas James Bridge and celebrate the efforts and achievements of the project. I congratulate contractors Civil Delaney, Hawkesbury City Council, Central Coast Council, Macdonald Valley Association and the community groups on their collaboration and perseverance in completing the project. A great sense of pride, accomplishment and connectedness to heritage was shared amongst attendees at the event.

On a similar note, I recently attended another momentous occasion in the Hawkesbury electorate. I joined students, staff and members of the community at Macdonald Valley Public School to acknowledge and celebrate the school's 180th anniversary. Current and former students came together to reflect on the school's long history and unique place in the heart of the valley. Carrying the distinction of being one of the oldest government schools in New South Wales, Macdonald Valley Public School inspires a strong sense of pride and connection among the students, which was very special to witness.

Principal Sarah Allen and the dedicated staff possess a clear passion for supporting their 13 students, ensuring their time at school is spent making strong friendships, partaking in meaningful learning engagements and connecting with the community. The celebration was a very special occasion that highlighted the projects and achievements of the students, who are clearly well supported, inspired and connected to their learning. I congratulate the students, staff and community of Macdonald Valley Public School on reaching that milestone, and I look forward to hearing about their future endeavours. I also recognise and congratulate Uncle Cole, who gave us a wonderful welcome to country and smoking ceremony on the day.

Our region continues to experience the pressures and pace of a changing world, but it is grounding to come together in moments that remind us of who we are, where we have come from and what binds our communities together. Those milestones highlight the strength that comes from honouring our heritage while looking confidently towards the future. Whether it is safeguarding our historic infrastructure or nurturing the next generation of learners, the Hawkesbury continues to show that progress and tradition are not opposing forces but partners in reshaping a thriving and connected community. I am deeply proud to represent an electorate where local history is cherished, community spirit is strong and our shared story continues to grow richer over time.

tree_branches.text:
Additionally, the rezonings provide the corridors for the road connections of Bandon Road, Garfield Road West and Townsend Road. To understand the significance of those precincts, it is important to understand how we got to this point. In May 2017 the North West Priority Growth Area Land Use and Infrastructure Implementation Plan was released. It stated:

When fully developed, the North West Priority Growth Area will accommodate approximately 90,000 homes, 20,000 more than were forecast in 2006.

The implementation plan set out to facilitate the supply of 18,000 new homes by 2021 and 33,000 new homes by 2026, with the remaining 57,000 homes to be built by 2036. It highlighted the need to balance the needs of a growing population with opportunities for employment and recreation by establishing minimum and maximum residential densities as a priority, in line with infrastructure provisions.

By the time I was elected, almost all of the rezoning for residential use had been completed, creating a pipeline of new housing developments that extended to 2036. A significant amount of development was underway, set to peak in 2027, but the precincts needed to create jobs and green space languished. The new homes were built, but employment opportunities, recreation space and infrastructure provision were ignored—so much so that around 84 per cent of workers living in the Riverstone electorate are forced to leave the area to get to their place of employment, due to a lack of local job infrastructure. We have the most youth and young families in New South Wales, but one of the largest green space deficits. Necessary infrastructure like schools, roads and public transport simply did not keep pace with the population growth. That is what our Government inherited, why I entered Parliament and what I am determined to fix.

In the case of Marsden Park North and West Schofields, the precincts plans were first put on public exhibition in 2018 proposing a combined 11,000 new homes. At the time I was vice-president of the North West Business Chamber and strongly opposed the plans because of the amount of homes being proposed in an area known to be flood prone. Flood studies from 2020 and 2022 also expressed concerns about the number of homes being proposed. Both precincts were put on hold pending the outcome of flood evacuation modelling [FEM], which was delivered to Government in late 2022 and released to the public in 2023. The FEM report found that if development was allowed to proceed under those plans, around 5,000 people could become trapped in a major flood event. Those unworkable precinct plans left landholders in a state of limbo with no pathway forward.

Our Government had little choice but to scrap the original proposals and come up with new plans, which caused a lot of anger and confusion for affected landholders but was necessary to deliver a workable solution. Starting from scratch created the opportunity to devise a plan that provided a framework for what was really needed—jobs, green space and the road infrastructure necessary to help unlock the region. In stark contrast to the former Liberal Government, which pursued rezonings for thousands of new homes with no ability to have them approved and little regard for the need to supplement housing with jobs, the Minns Labor Government listened to experts, council, emergency services and, most importantly, the community. We understand that development needs more than just housing to create communities.

We are investing in the infrastructure that our area needs, with upgrades to roads like Bandon Road, Garfield Road East, Garfield Road West and Townson Road, as well as the Richmond Road upgrade between the M7 and Townson Road. There are nine new schools and many more being upgraded from Box Hill in the east to Marsden Park in the west. We have added over 160 new buses. The final business case for the Tallawong to St Marys metro is expected early next year. Those are not future promises; they are already underway. I note that West Schofields and Marsden Park North are not in the Riverstone electorate, but I have been working with the planning Minister since being elected to Parliament because they are part of my community and have a profound effect on my constituents. I say to the residents of Riverstone, Marsden Park North and West Schofields that their needs have been prioritised. After years of being told to wait, an achievable plan for the future is being proposed. I urge all residents to make a submission via the Planning Portal during the public exhibition period of these plans to make sure their voices are heard so that we can get the possible outcome for our area into the future.

For over a year, the Brookvale P&C has raised legitimate concerns about high school catchment boundaries. Currently, Brookvale Public School falls in the catchment area for the Northern Beaches Secondary College Cromer Campus without access to local single sex school options. The department has said that will continue, even though the nearby Northern Beaches Secondary College Freshwater Senior Campus is transitioning to a comprehensive years 7 to 12 high school from 2027 and the new Forest High School is opening in Allambie Height, the suburb right next door. The clear request from the Brookvale P&C is to include Brookvale in the intake area for the new years 7 to 12 Freshwater campus. I am also keen to see maximum choice for Brookvale families, including opening up Forest High School, Mackellar Girls Campus and Balgowlah Boys' Campus.

There are several reasons why keeping Brookvale zoned to Cromer campus is illogical and including it in the Freshwater catchment makes a lot more sense. Firstly, is geographic accessibility: Freshwater campus will be the closest high school, just 1.4 kilometres away from Brookvale Public School. It is mostly flat and a walkable or rideable distance from home for many Brookvale students. Cromer campus is much further away, involving a longer and more complex commute of up to 45 minutes, including multiple bus transfers. Over six years of high school that is about 1,800 hours commuting, equivalent to almost a full school year spent just travelling.

Secondly, is about maintaining community connectedness. Listening to the parent body at Brookvale, the reality is their networks of sports and social activities are the same as the families who will attend the Freshwater campus. Brookvale children train and play with Brookvale Football Club in Manly, play netball at Curl Curl, or are members of Surf Life Saving clubs at Freshwater and Curl Curl, among countless other engagements. We need to encourage continuity and depth of social connection, for both parents and students, across different parts of their lives. Thirdly, and very importantly, there is a fairness, equity and inclusion dimension to this issue. The position statement from Brookvale P&C states:

The decision to exclude Brookvale from the Freshwater Campus intake also appears to deepen class-based inequalities in the Northern Beaches public school system. Brookvale is home to a far more diverse mix of ethnic, cultural, and socio-economic backgrounds than many surrounding suburbs. Yet, we are being cut off from the high school options being made available to wealthier areas like Freshwater, Curl Curl, Manly and Balgowlah.

Brookvale students and families should get the same choices and opportunities as surrounding suburbs. Brookvale is a small school, so we are talking about a low number of students each year, which will have minimal impact on numbers at the Freshwater campus. The Brookvale Public School community feels that, in both process and outcome, the current high school zoning decision is unjustified and unfair. Frankly, I agree with them. I will not go into the details, but I think the Department of Education could have been more responsive and transparent on this issue.

I thank the members of the P&C, particularly president Hina Osmany, for being so engaged, eloquent and persistent in their advocacy. Brookvale is a small school doing great things. It needs to be celebrated, maintained and supported, not undermined. I have made clear to the education Minister's office my strong view that Brookvale primary students should be zoned for Freshwater campus from day one in 2027. Depending on capacity, I also think Brookvale students should have the option of Forest High, Mackellar Girls or Balgowlah Boys. I have also sought and received the following commitments from the education Minister's office: firstly, for the education Minister to meet with the P&C leadership before the beginning of the 2026 school year; secondly, for an expression of interest survey process for students in years 4, 5 and 6 at Brookvale to get an accurate picture of their high school preferences and the numbers of students; and, thirdly, at the very least for there to be a catchment review in 2027, taking into account actual enrolments across all schools impacted by the zoning changes. However, I am pushing for this to happen in late 2026 so that, if possible, students can start at their preferred high school in 2027.

I have also requested that if Brookvale students are not included in the Freshwater campus catchment from day one in 2027, they should have formal out‑of‑area enrolment priority at Freshwater, Forest High, Mackellar Girls and Balgowlah Boys. I will continue to push for this and keep the community updated. School catchment boundaries may be lines on a map for the Department of Education, but for students and families these are life‑changing delineations. Decisions about school catchments need to be made with local insight and proper consultation. The wrong call has been made in this case, and I will keep pushing for a fairer, commonsense outcome for Brookvale families.

Our churches play an equally important role. We are fortunate to have many active congregations across our electorate, each running their own internal Christmas donation drives. These groups quietly collect food, gifts and supplies to ensure that families doing it tough feel supported. Organisations like Georges River Life Care continue their year-round support. This year it is again running its "light, hope, joy, strength" Christmas appeal. This provides practical help and emotional support to people who need it most. Another inspiring example of East Hills community spirit is the partnership between Picnic Point High School and Keith's Closet. The Picnic Point High School community came together to deliver more than 30 boxes filled with toiletries and accessories for people accessing mental health services. Every item was thoughtfully wrapped, a simple gesture that will make someone's Christmas a little brighter. The community even dedicated a full day to packing, giving students and families a hands-on opportunity to support others. Keith's Closet's Christmas drives and annual Shoebox Appeal are now in their fifth year. The organisation is aiming for 1,000 boxes and is well on its way. Its work has brought comfort and hope to countless people across Sydney and the East Hills electorate.

Our businesses are also stepping up. The Canterbury Bankstown Chamber of Commerce is running its annual Christmas toy drive, bringing the local business community together to give every child the chance to feel the joy of the season. The efforts of the chamber and local businesses show how strongly our small business owners care for the families they serve. It is such a privilege to be able to deliver these toys to sick kids at our local hospital, bringing a small bit of joy to those facing some of the toughest moments of their young lives. Groups like Anglicare, through initiatives such as Toys 'n' Tucker, continue to support local households with food and presents, making sure Christmas can be a time of celebration, not stress.

We also see this community spirit shine through in our local Christmas carols. Panania Anglican Church is once again hosting their Christmas carols event, bringing together families, neighbours and parish members to celebrate the season in song. Over at Rotary Club of Padstow, they are preparing for their much-loved Carols by Candlelight. This family event continues to draw a huge crowd every year. It has become one of the biggest and most anticipated community gatherings. It lights up the season and gives families a chance to come together in a joyful and meaningful way.

All of these examples show that the East Hills electorate is built on generosity, community and genuine care for others. This spirit is not limited to one organisation or one suburb. It is seen throughout Panania, Revesby, Padstow, East Hills, Condell Park, Georges Hall and every corner of our electorate. I am delighted to formally acknowledge my own Christmas card competition winner, Timothy Zhang, from Panania North Public School. His beautiful Christmas design, including a very Aussie Santa, will be in letterboxes throughout our community very soon.

As we move towards the end of the year, I acknowledge every volunteer, every school, every community organisation or group, every business, every faith organisation, and every family who has contributed to these efforts. They are the reason East Hills remains such a strong, supportive and deeply connected community. To everyone who has given their time, their donations, or simply a moment of kindness, I say thank you for making our electorate a great place to live, and reminding us what community means. I wish everyone a safe and happy holiday season, spent with family and friends, or the person that cares for them most.

tree_branches.name: Tribute to Robert Gray
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Tribute to Robert Gray
tree_branches.text:
Now the mind is turned down, like a gas flame in a dark kitchen

Where the wind and all the night sounds can be heard.

It lies once more beneath the truth of the body.

All of my demanding

Has become, crossing these paddocks, and watching the other stars appear,

As delicate as the first mould on black bread, simply to take an axe and go on

Up to the end of the cleared land, underneath

The hooded eucalyptus forest,

To crack some firewood

From a weather tightened grey log,

For a hot, deep bath, that I can draw out through the evening.

Robert would say of his poetry:

My poetry is full of images, because I want to particularise every natural thing that appears in it, out of respect, you might say. In my poems, nothing is a symbol for anything else. Everything has its own worth and is presented directly. The overall effect is one of clarity and light.

Robert was gifted in life with a great love story, sharing his life for over 50 years with his partner, Dee Jones. Robert's final years were not easy. He had a long struggle with Parkinson's. In fact, that is how I came to know of Robert, when Dee reached out to me and my office last year. Robert had been stuck at St Vincent's Hospital for 31 days waiting for an aged‑care bed. Unfortunately, Robert's story is not unique. When a bed was eventually found it was in Bass Hill, far from home, far from his friends and far from Dee. It would have meant Dee travelling a three-hour round trip on public transport to see him every day.

My office, along with Robert's friends, like Peter Goldsworthy, worked hard and managed to find Robert a bed closer to home at Uniting in Waverley. His final days were spent with Dee by his side. In the last 11 months of his life, Dee would spend over five hours every day by his side, feeding him by hand and reading to him. There is some sad irony but also beauty in the fact that Robert's most human poem, In Departing Light , captured the pain of watching a loved one slip away. It recounts the final days of his mother's struggle with Alzheimer's. I want to end by reading from part of that poem:

But why become so fearful?

This is all

of your mother, in your arms. She who now, a moment after your game, has gone;

who is confused

and would like to ask

why she is hanging here. No—she will be safe. She will be safe

in the dry mouth

of this red earth, in the place

she has always been. She

who hasn't survived living, how can we dream that she will survive her death?

Now Robert Gray returns to that red earth, his ashes to be scattered where his mother's were. Vale, Robert Gray, a great Australian.

tree_branches.text:
Across the Central Coast, community groups, services, council and government agencies, including police, are working together to shine a light on this issue. This year's 16 Days of Activism includes a series of powerful events including: the annual walk against domestic violence, where community members come together in solidarity wearing orange to signal a future free from violence; public art installations in Gosford, symbolic houses suspended in Kibble Park and flowers honouring victims and survivors; yarn-bombing displays by the Zonta group, drawing attention to the many forms violence can take; a preview of a new children's storybook promoting healthy, respectful relationships from an early age; and awareness banners displayed prominently across Gosford, Tuggerah and surrounding town centres.

Importantly, this year we add a significant community event in my electorate, the No to Domestic Violence Walk in Toukley on 27 November. This walk is a powerful grassroots initiative, bringing families, local businesses, sporting clubs and service providers together on the streets of Toukley to say, "No more. Not here, not anywhere." It demonstrates the strength, unity and compassion of the northern Central Coast community. I encourage everyone who can to attend. Showing up matters. Visibility matters. Solidarity matters. Alongside these community-led actions, the New South Wales Government continues to invest in new supports, including a new Core and Cluster refuge on the Central Coast, grants for prevention activities, and programs that focus on engaging men as allies in changing harmful attitudes and behaviours.

It is a shared call to action, so what can each of us do not only during these 16 days but throughout the year? We can speak up: If you are worried about someone, reach out. Silence is not protection. We can show up: Attend events like the Toukley walk on 27 November, or the Central Coast-wide Walk Against Domestic Violence. We can educate: Have the difficult conversations at home, at work and in sporting clubs. We can support services: Local organisations are doing life-saving work and need our backing. We can be an ally, especially for men and boys: Call out disrespect, challenge harmful behaviour and model positive relationships. The 16 Days of Activism remind us that change starts with community. It starts with all of us choosing respect, choosing kindness, choosing to intervene and choosing to stand alongside those affected by violence. On the Central Coast we are strong, we are caring, and together we can ensure that every home is a safe home.

As a father of two daughters, one 23 and one 25, I am always particularly concerned that they will be in healthy, respectful relationships. But it does not matter. Our young women and mothers sometimes fall prey to people who have records of disrespectful relationships. So, as a community, we must always keep an eye out. I call out the Toukley RSL Club, the Ary, whose workers wear purple T-shirts every week to show their support for the fight against domestic violence and for being a safe place for women to be informed or to seek out help with domestic violence. I urge all members to get involved in the 16 Days of Activism.

We have some fantastic hospitals. We are building the Moree Hospital and the Glen Innes Hospital is yet to start. But our main problem is staffing. As a State Parliament, we need to lean heavily on the Federal Parliament so that it removes the blocks that are causing difficulties in regional healthcare recruitment. We need more training places for doctors. The University of New England is in my electorate and could train hundreds more doctors every year but for the restriction on its intake. As a State Parliament, we need to look at that.

Crime is an ongoing problem in my electorate, particularly at the western end, in towns such as Moree, Mungindi and Inverell. Unfortunately, it is multilayered and predominantly youth crime. We now have a situation where elderly residents in towns like Moree, my home town, go to bed at night in fear. As a Parliament, we need to do more, particularly about the courts. Some of the bail decisions I have seen this year, particularly for young offenders, are completely out of kilter with the community's expectations. We are having a debate tomorrow on the Government's bill about the doli incapax test, and I thank the Government for bringing it back in. I cannot believe Government members are taking selfies and not listening to my wonderful statement.

Another issue for my electorate is road maintenance. I give credit to the roads Minister and thank the Minister and her staff for listening to me. Like the health Minister and his staff, they are probably sick to death of emails and phone calls from me, but our roads took an absolute hammering during the east coast low that hit earlier in the year and again in the snowstorm throughout New England. It is good to see those State roads being fixed, slowly but surely. The problem with my electorate's roads is that the local councils' road networks are simply too big for them to manage. The State Parliament and Federal Parliament should have a bigger discussion about how to fund regional councils, because the road networks are simply too big for the rate base and a local council can put up rates only so many times before it is voted out. As a Parliament, we need to look at that.

A more recent problem that has raised its head in my electorate is that of renewables. Over the past probably 12 months, renewables have been relatively quiet. However, EnergyCo's decision to reroute the transmission line from Bayswater through to Walcha has caused massive unrest and brought to a head a number of issues with the renewables rollout. I often say that regional people are not against renewables. We are happy to do our part and have our share. But what we do not like is feeling as though we are being absolutely blindsided and rolled over—for want of a better phrase—by the rollout.

I note that the planning laws are 45 years out of date. In a perfect world, we would have a separate piece of legislation that would trump the existing planning laws and carve out the rights, the obligations and the process for large-scale renewables in regional and rural areas. If we could do that, if regional people were listened to and worked with and if councils had a say in where these projects go, it would take much of the heat out of the debate. People talk about cumulative impact. It would be wise for us as a Parliament to look at a legislative requirement for studies on cumulative impact before developments start. Again, it is not that we are against renewables; it is that the rollout is not being done fairly.

tree_branches.text:
In November 1980 members of the Pontian Association of NSW purchased the property in Earlwood, which was then a greyhound-training facility. The property was quickly renovated and became the community hall we now know as the Pontian House. For many years the Pontian House has proudly promoted Pontian culture, serving as a place where like-minded Pontian Greeks with a passion for their culture and history can keep the Pontian spirit alive in New South Wales. The Pontic Greek community has always been proud of its heritage, as are most Greek communities. The story of the Pontic Greeks is one of resilience and perseverance. The Pontians have always shown an unwavering commitment to preserving their culture and history through adversity, particularly during the truly horrific Pontic genocide, which occurred during World War I and its aftermath.

It is because of this adversity that Pontic Greeks across the world strive to protect and celebrate their culture. In Australia the Pontian Association of NSW has helped to preserve and promote the Pontic culture, legacy, history, language, dance and many traditions. The Pontian House is a beacon of cultural continuity. It is more than just a meeting place for Pontic Greeks. One of the most significant cultural activities at the Pontian House is the free dance lessons offered to people of all ages: children, young people, adults and the elderly. Different generations of Pontians come together to learn and perform traditional Pontian dances. This wonderful intergenerational activity ensures that Pontian culture is remembered, passed on and celebrated. It is a meaningful way for generations of Pontic Greeks to immerse themselves in their culture.

I acknowledge the hard work of the Pontian Greeks. Almost all the Pontians I know in my electorate and across New South Wales are hard working, industrious and entrepreneurial. But, more importantly, they have contributed much to the advancement of Australia and of New South Wales, ensuring that there is peace and prosperity among not only Greek Australians but also Australians of different faiths and ethnicities. They are always at the forefront. If there are concerns or issues in our community, the Pontian Greeks, along with many of the leaders in my community, come together because, at the end of the day, social cohesion is important in our community. The Pontian Greeks come together on solemn occasions and annually commemorate what happened to their ancestors during the genocide, which was a very difficult period. For many, that is in their spirit and soul. I am very proud to be their representative and to learn the stories of their parents and grandparents, who were pioneers and did something very special in our community. The grandkids, the third and fourth generation kids, are learning the language, dance and ancient instruments as well.

I acknowledge everyone involved in the Pontian community of New South Wales and with the Pontian House. I congratulate and give a very special mention to the hardworking Maria Anthony, the president of the Pontian Association of NSW, and her amazing committee. I am very much looking forward to attending the forty‑fifth celebrations. I thank president Maria Anthony for inviting me. I congratulate her and commend the committee and the volunteers for their enormous contribution to New South Wales.

tree_branches.text:
Their actions every day ensure that The Greens are in this Parliament and that I am in this House as the member for Newtown putting a different agenda forward that does not subscribe to the idea of caving in to the powers that seek to control our democracy and our society. The work behind the scenes that allows social change often goes unseen: It is the people who will rock up as volunteers with a portable megaphone to a rally, the volunteers who traipse the streets putting things in letterboxes and the people who text others to check they are okay when they are being trolled on social media by vile individuals who seek to shut down social change in our communities.

I recognise that social change and politics is very hard. Some of the people—whether they are the amazing humans in the electorate office of Newtown or the activists seeking to push the boundaries to get justice for First Nations people, trans people and so many communities that are under attack, including public housing residents in this State—go above and beyond in addition to their day jobs to push for a better world for all of us. I do not say very often that I was not a radical before I moved to Newtown. I remember being at a share house party in the heart of the electorate of Newtown at the age of 19, having a fight with someone because I did not understand the point of a rally. I know that would be hard for members to believe—

TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Alex Greenwich ): No-one believes it.

Ms JENNY LEONG: —but I did not know why anyone would bother marching on the street. I did not understand the reason for that. Maybe my very measured Adelaide upbringing brought that to bear. I acknowledge that it was the good activists, lefties and radicals of Newtown who taught me the value of collective power, collective organising and practical solidarity. With the education they gave me, I hope that I can offer that same support to others to recognise that solidarity and support are not just words and that the privilege of going to a rally or speaking on behalf of communities in this Chamber should not be taken lightly.

I hope I can repay every practical act of solidarity and support that I have experienced since being the member for Newtown to others as we continue to push for much-needed reforms, whether that is dealing with the climate crisis, the inequality crisis, the lack of housing justice in our city or the lack of treaties for First Nations people. Those are collective and intersectional struggles, and we have an obligation and a responsibility to deliver on them. The member for Sydney is in the chair, and the other day I was reflecting on the fact that we first met in 2007 when I ran for the Federal electorate of Sydney. We know more than anyone how long the struggles have been going on for and how much we need to stay focused on the collective struggles to enact the change we are trying to achieve.

tree_branches.name: Northern Beaches Hospital
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Northern Beaches Hospital
tree_branches.text:
It is clear that there is broad community and professional support for the Government assuming responsibility for the delivery of public health services. But the question before us, and one that remains unanswered, is what will happen to private health services on the northern beaches? The Northern Beaches Hospital performs around 20,000 private procedures each year across disciplines including orthopaedics, cardiology, neurosurgery, oncology, urology, vascular care and mental health care. Those services are essential components of an integrated health system that combines public and private care to meet the diverse needs of patients.

Local clinicians have expressed to me that any loss of private capacity could have significant consequences. Private hospitals perform the majority of elective surgeries in New South Wales. Removing that capacity from the northern beaches will push thousands of patients back into the public system, which is already under significant strain. Public waitlists will grow and then the flow-on effects will be felt well beyond our community on the northern beaches. Many medical professionals have written to me expressing their alarm at both the process and the potential outcomes. One specialist wrote to me, saying:

While we fully support the NSW Government taking back responsibility for public services, the potential loss of access to a private hospital on the Northern Beaches would be a very poor outcome. There has been very little consultation or public awareness of this possibility. Why should residents here be denied access to the same private services available to other parts of Sydney - The Mater, St Vincent's, or North Shore Private?

Another specialist wrote to me, saying:

The issue is the continuation of access to services for the residents of the Northern Beaches. Even if the Minister keeps his promise of maintaining a level 5 hospital, that does not ensure access to private health facilities, choice of doctor, or the continuation of specialist procedures that are not available in the public system.

Those concerns are reasonable and are echoed by numerous medical specialists who live and work in our community. They are not driven by politics; they are driven by what they see every day: the needs of patients. The Northern Beaches Hospital has built a strong reputation for integrated care, with public and private clinicians working side by side to deliver excellent outcomes. That model has resulted in some of the best surgical wait‑time performances in the State, with no breaches of elective surgery targets year after year.

As those clinicians have told me, removing private capacity risks dismantling that model of excellence. It would jeopardise vital specialist services in cancer surgery; robotic and minimally invasive procedures; cardiac and vascular care; and private mental health programs. For families, it could mean the loss of private maternity and paediatric services. For older residents, it could mean travelling long distances for orthopaedic, spinal or vascular surgery. It is vital that whatever changes occur, the principles of accessibility, integration and choice are maintained. Our community values being able to receive both public and private care locally, without needing to travel long distances for essential treatment.

It is not about politics; it is about patients. It is about respecting the doctors, nurses and healthcare staff, who work tirelessly to provide the best possible outcomes. It is about ensuring that residents of the northern beaches have the same healthcare choices as every other community in Sydney. Therefore, I urge the Government to continue engaging closely with local clinicians, hospital staff and community representatives as it determines the hospital's future structure. Their insights and experience are invaluable, and ensuring their voices are heard will help maintain confidence and continuity for patients. The northern beaches community deserves clarity about the future of its healthcare, and confidence that both public and private services will remain accessible, high quality and close to home.

tree_branches.text:
There was also a horrific series of home invasions carried out by one young man earlier this year, including two where elderly ladies were raped. There is also the ongoing issue of organised crime and some high-profile incidents, including where a car was set upon at the traffic lights on Church Street in Parramatta on the boundary of my electorate and that of the member for Parramatta. Fairly recently, a person's house was shot at, but they were not the intended target, so the house of the intended target was shot at a few days later. People are concerned that organised crime is perhaps not as organised as it used to be and that things are being outsourced to people who are brazen but not very accurate about the people they target. That has resulted in mistaken identity murders and people's houses being shot up when they are not the intended victim. Those things have made people in my community very concerned of late.

I regularly run community surveys. Crime does not usually rate in the top three issues, but lately it has because of those horrific crimes. On Monday night a number of people came together to talk about issues that are of particular concern to them. They were not necessarily the issues around organised crime, but there are a number of things that have been worrying people in my community. An ongoing issue, which is not limited to my area, is people riding trail bikes through parks and, more recently, the use of e-bikes to do the same thing on footpaths, which is causing other people all sorts of distress. That is difficult for the police to deal with because, by the time they arrive, the people riding the bikes have long since departed.

During the course of the evening, information was passed through about the interception of the "kill car" in Merrylands West, which is also in my electorate. Just a five-minute drive from where we held the forum, a member of the public saw some young men wearing balaclavas jump in a car and start acting strange. The person filmed them and immediately submitted it to the police. An arrest was made, and weapons and jerry cans were found in the car. That foiled either kidnappings or possibly worse. It was a good result. I cannot speak more highly of the Cumberland Police Area Command. Whenever I ask about crimes that people are particularly worried about, arrests are nearly always made within a couple of days.

I thank the police Minister for providing us with an additional 15 probationary constables this year. We certainly need the extra workforce. There is plenty of work to be done in my area. They are certainly getting to work on making the arrests that are needed. We need to do more to make people aware of how to avoid crime and report crime, and feel more comfortable doing that. In some countries the police are the biggest criminals in town, so we must help people feel comfortable reporting crime. That is done very well in my community.

tree_branches.name: Orange Electorate
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Orange Electorate
tree_branches.text:
A central pillar of my advocacy this year was pushing for the installation of a da Vinci surgical robot at the Orange Health Service. Through formal motions in Parliament, I highlighted the clear benefits of robotic surgery, which provides greater precision, minimally invasive procedures, shorter recovery times, fewer complications and better outcomes for patients. The robust business case already exists and demonstrates the need to bring regional surgical capability in line with metropolitan standards. That advocacy is about quality and equity, and ensuring that Central West patients can access modern surgical care close to home.

Workforce is also important. Advanced equipment helps to attract and retain specialist surgeons, particularly in urology, where regional workforce pressures are acute. As a result of my sustained lobbying, the Western NSW Local Health District has agreed to reassess the viability of delivering robotic surgery through its new clinical services plan. That is long-term reform, but I remain steadfast that regional patients deserve cutting‑edge care, like those in the city. Transport and regional infrastructure also remained major priorities. After sustained advocacy, I was able to secure a significant breakthrough: A $2 million Government commitment to plan a passenger train stabling facility in Orange. That is an important step towards restoring daily return passenger rail services between Orange and Sydney, and improving reliable transport links across the Central West.

This year, I continued championing virtual fencing, including during debate on the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Amendment (Virtual Stock Fencing) Bill 2023. That work contributed to the New South Wales Government agreeing to legalise virtual stock fencing. Using GPS-enabled collars to contain livestock without physical fences, virtual fencing offers major benefits. Those benefits include reduced fencing and maintenance costs, improved pasture management, real-time animal monitoring and increased farm safety. That reform will modernise livestock management in New South Wales and provide producers with a more efficient and sustainable tool for the future. It will be an absolute game changer for the industry.

Recovery from the devastating Central West floods has remained one of my highest priorities. As both local MP for many of the affected communities and chair of the Central West Community Leaders Forum, I continued working closely with councils and local leaders to push for fair, sustained investment, particularly for damaged water and sewer infrastructure that is essential to long-term resilience. That lobbying resulted in more than $20 million in funding for the Parkes, Cabonne and Lachlan shires. I have closely monitored the implementation of recovery programs, including the Resilient Homes Program, to ensure that assistance reaches those most in need. Rebuilding strengthens communities against future disasters.

Mental health has remained an important area of focus, particularly regarding decisions of the Mental Health Review Tribunal, or the MHRT, relating to forensic patients. Throughout 2025, I have raised concerns that too many tribunal decisions appear to favour patients' liberties over the safety and rights of registered victims in the broader community. In Parliament I moved an amendment to the Mental Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2024 to require electronic monitoring, such as GPS ankle bracelets, for forensic patients who are granted leave. That was about public safety and restoring trust in a system that has long operated with limited transparency.

Law and order remain front and centre. Early this year I called for a return of 24-hour policing in Forbes. A strong local police presence is essential for deterrence and rapid response. The tragic domestic violence homicide of Forbes mother and early childhood educator Molly Ticehurst underscores the urgent need for around‑the‑clock policing to improve response capability. Finally, I note there will be expansion to palliative care services. That expansion will open in January, with an increase to five beds, and $21 million has been provided for a new operating theatre at Forbes hospital, which was announced in this year's State budget.

tree_branches.name: First Guardian and Shield Master Funds
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > First Guardian and Shield Master Funds
tree_branches.text:
In recent months, ASIC has launched significant enforcement action in response to what it described as "industrial‑scale misconduct". It has launched action against InterPrac Financial Planning for failing to ensure its representatives act in its clients' best interests and for facilitating more than $600 million in super investments in First Guardian and Shield. It has launched action against Ferras Merhi for allegedly directing clients into these schemes, while receiving almost $40 million in fees, commissions and marketing payments. It has also taken action against SQM Research for allegedly issuing favourable ratings of high-risk products in ways that ASIC says misled consumers.

These actions, some of which ASIC has described as "first of their kind", highlight the scale of systemic failure and the growing scrutiny of the broader network of financial actors that enabled these funds to reach mainstream superannuation platforms. One of the most serious issues is how easily First Guardian and Shield were able to appear on major superannuation platforms, including Macquarie Wrap, Netwealth, OneVue and AMP's North. The inclusion of these funds on mainstream platforms gave them the perception of credibility and drove inflows from advisers and consumers alike. Macquarie, under regulatory pressure from ASIC, has agreed to fully reimburse Shield investors on its platform. That is a $321 million commitment.

Other platforms should seriously consider following Macquarie's lead. The scandal is not the fault of one government, regulator or era. It has been decades in the making under multiple regulatory regimes. The deeper problem is structural. The industry is riddled with inherent conflicts. Funds rely on platforms to distribute products, platforms rely on advisers to drive inflows, and advisers rely on commissions and incentives. All of these depend on research houses, which are paid by the very funds they are meant to assess. Every link in the chain is conflicted, and those conflicts ultimately left consumers last.

Victims and advocacy groups have been very clear about their demands. They want to see an expansion and strengthening of the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort so that victims have access to redress. They want to see the adoption of a pay now, recover later model, as used in the HIH collapse and the National Redress Scheme, whereby government compensates the victims upfront and then recovers funds from those responsible—the trustees, licensees, product issuers, research houses and potentially their directors. They want to see the strengthening of governance and accountability by enforcing platform and trustee transparency, holding research houses to account, and banning conflicted remuneration for high-risk products.

Finally, they would like to see a full parliamentary inquiry. I also called for that earlier this year when I spoke about this issue. We must examine how First Guardian and Shield bypassed oversight, how they accessed major platforms, how trustee and research house scrutiny failed, how hundreds of millions of dollars were moved offshore, and how this conduct escaped ASIC, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre despite repeated red flags.

At the centre of that scandal are everyday Australians who did nothing wrong. They are teachers, retail workers, carers and tradespeople who entrusted their futures to a system that promised security. Instead, their savings were used to buy sports cars and fund lavish lifestyles and were channelled offshore, far from the reach of ordinary Australians. The only just outcome is for most, if not all, of those victims' funds to be recovered. They were let down by a system that claimed to safeguard them. It is now that system's responsibility to deliver justice, reform and accountability.

tree_branches.name: Narrandera Water Infrastructure
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Narrandera Water Infrastructure
tree_branches.text:
Too often what comes out is a brown liquid that, whilst meeting Australian Drinking Water Guidelines, looks, tastes and smells putrid. For the almost 4,000 residents and hundreds of local businesses already dealing with recurring episodes of discoloured, foul-tasting water, the hot, dry summer ahead brings a genuine fear that the town's ageing water infrastructure simply will not cope. Boil water alerts are once again a very real possibility. It is plain that families should not have to watch brown water flow from their taps, wondering whether it is safe to drink, cook with or bathe their children in.

That is why I have written to the Minister for Water seeking urgent short-term measures to protect the community ahead of and throughout the summer. I have called for the deployment of a mobile, temporary water treatment plant for Narrandera, configured to deal with colour and taste problems by removing iron, manganese and the compounds that cause odour. I have also requested $2 million in State funding so that Narrandera Shire Council can flush the town's water mains before peak demand, giving households confidence that, when they turn the tap, clean water will come out. Whilst a permanent solution is more time critical than ever, those practical steps—which represent stopgap measures only—would show that the Government understands the urgency of the situation.

The former Coalition Government created and funded the $1 billion Safe and Secure Water program, designed to deliver exactly the kind of permanent solution Narrandera needs. I have spoken ad nauseam about that program over the past eight years. Fundamentally, Narrandera needs a modern water treatment plant. Work to fix the issue was well underway before the change of government. The former Government funded scoping work for a permanent filtration plant through the Safe and Secure Water program and committed further support for critical projects in Narrandera's water and sewer network. The Integrated Water Cycle Management strategy proposal was underway as NSW Labor came to government. The project cost of $30 million, which was later revised to $37 million, has been publicly known for almost 12 months.

I acknowledge that the current Government has supported council's bid to the National Water Grid Fund for detailed design work on a new filtration plant, and we eagerly await the outcome of that application. But we cannot shy away from the fact that detailed design and construction is not yet funded and, even when it is, will take years to build. Narrandera needs both long-term solutions and immediate help to get safely through this summer. Disappointingly, instead of building on the momentum created by the Coalition's Safe and Secure Water program, the Labor Government now concedes that the fund is fully allocated and has chosen not to top it up, even as critical projects across rural New South Wales become more urgent by the day.

In the case of Narrandera, during her first visit to the region in June 2023, the Minister for Water promised to fast-track plans for a new water treatment plant for Narrandera, yet 2½ years later there is still no funding announcement and no timetable for delivery. The inaction of the Government is unacceptable. The people of Narrandera deserve better treatment than they have received so far. I urge the Minister for Water and the Premier to approve the temporary treatment plant, fund the mains flushing program and then match the longer term commitment demonstrated by the Commonwealth and the local council. It is time to deliver the safe, clean drinking water that every Australian is entitled to expect. As the member for Cootamundra, I will continue to support Narrandera until that basic promise is fulfilled.

tree_branches.name: Greyhound Racing NSW
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Greyhound Racing NSW
tree_branches.text:
The objectives of Greyhound Racing NSW do not consider the social and cultural role that the sport plays in regional communities and the local economic impacts of its actions. It is more lost amenity and lost opportunity for social and family activity in regional New South Wales. The way the criteria were designed was always going to disadvantage regional and non-TAB track facilities. I believe that was intentional. The recommendations from Deloitte were predetermined by the criteria that were used.

My communities of Coonamble and Broken Hill have a strong and active group of greyhound enthusiasts. The rug was pulled from under their feet when they were told that they are being considered for closure in June 2026. Coonamble has experienced mixed messaging from Greyhound Racing NSW about its future, the annual Coonamble carnival and the works required to bring the track up to a standard that many other tracks still in use do not meet. Greyhound racing is an important part of the fabric of the Coonamble community, and the carnival is an important drawcard that drives people and money to Coonamble.

If the track at Broken Hill ceases to race, participants will go to Adelaide rather than New South Wales. The more they are on the road, the higher the chance of an accident. Dogs do not always do well after hours on the road in a trailer. I wonder if Greyhound Racing NSW has considered the welfare implications of making dogs travel. The criteria and weighting made it impossible to recommend Broken Hill continue because it has no surrounding communities within a 150-kilometre radius. It chooses not to race in the summer for welfare reasons. It is looking after the dogs.

Given the short time frame until closure in June, there is concern that no investment will be made in the last season. Many of the dogs would end up in the Greyhounds As Pets program. The design of the criteria and weighting system really set small clubs up to fail. Broken Hill has the infrastructure and the dogs, and the business is profitable. Broken Hill has never been told it is at risk and was given no option to negotiate. It is willing to make changes and accommodate changes. It has also been told previously that it is meeting or exceeding any benchmark it is required to.

I have heard examples of clubs that are banding together to offer support to other clubs. I would like to see that support from Greyhound Racing NSW. After 52 years as a club and 48 years as a non-TAB club, the last two years for Broken Hill have been spent contributing to the industry through TAB events. Under the current Greyhound Racing NSW approach, tracks like Broken Hill and Coonamble will be lost in regional areas. It is not just happening in Barwon. Tracks in Nowra, Tamworth, Maitland, Wentworth Park, Kempsey, Wagga Wagga, Young, Potts Park, Wauchope and Moree are all being considered for closure. The discussions I have had with greyhound trainers and racers suggest that it will certainly lead to people exiting the industry. They will not go to the trouble and expense of traveling for hours with dogs to other tracks.

What needs to happen? Any decision to close tracks needs to be put on hold pending a parliamentary inquiry into Greyhound Racing NSW and its actions. Scrutiny and accountability needs to be applied through the Parliament. The terms of reference for an inquiry should include the objectives of Greyhound Racing NSW and its suitability; equity of access to Greyhound Racing NSW funds for regional clubs; the support offered by Greyhound Racing NSW to smaller regional track facilities; the role and objectives of the Greyhound Welfare Integrity Commission; greyhound welfare measures, including rehoming programs; and financial decisions of Greyhound Racing NSW, including contract employment arrangements. The objectives of Greyhound Racing NSW need to be expanded to consider the social, cultural and economic factors that are impacted by its decisions. I will therefore seek to amend the governing legislation to ensure that the holistic impacts of decisions by Greyhound Racing NSW need to be a factor in those decisions. I ask every member in Parliament to support continued greyhound racing in regional New South Wales.

tree_branches.name: Road Tolls
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Private Members' Statements > Road Tolls
tree_branches.text:
For more than 50 years motorists have paid only one‑way tolls on the Sydney Harbour road crossings. The Harbour Bridge was tolled in both directions when it opened in 1932 but, once the bridge had been paid off, the northbound toll was scrapped way back in 1970. The Harbour Tunnel has likewise been paid off. These crossings belong to the people of New South Wales. Yet Labor now wants to turn them back into a two‑way tax on Sydney motorists despite all their sound and fury in opposition to road tolls. This comes during one of the most difficult cost‑of‑living periods in living memory. Families are tightening their belts, renters and mortgage holders are under immense pressure, and small businesses are struggling with rising costs. People are already paying more for groceries, fuel and utilities and now, incredibly, Labor wants to make it more expensive just to get to work.

For a teacher driving across the bridge to an early shift, a nurse heading home after a night on the ward at Royal North Shore Hospital, a tradie moving tools to a city job site, or parents shuttling kids to activities, Labor's broken promise will mean paying twice to make the same journey. That is a doubling of their toll burden, a doubling of pressure on people who simply cannot afford more. And why? Because the Government cannot manage its budget. Because, instead of providing real cost‑of‑living solutions, they reach for the easiest revenue lever and hope motorists will not notice. This is a lazy revenue grab that punishes ordinary people.

No‑one should be surprised. Labor has form on this. For decades, they have treated Sydney motorists as a bottomless source of toll revenue. In fact, around half of Sydney's toll road network was commissioned or delivered under Labor governments. The Sydney Harbour Tunnel, the M2, the Eastern Distributor, the Cross City Tunnel, the Westlink M7 and the Lane Cove Tunnel—all toll roads approved, commissioned or opened by Labor. And none symbolises Labor's tolling record more than the tolled Military Road ramps in my community. It is a toll on a 200-metre on and off ramp between two completely toll‑free roads. It is one of the most expensive stretches of road in the world and must be one of the worst tolling decisions ever made. My community is slugged just to join or leave a freeway.

And now we see history repeating itself. The Premier is once again reaching for the motorist's hip pocket. He wants to toll both directions across the harbour, doubling the charge on infrastructure that was paid for decades ago. Instead of genuine reform, this Government delivered a toll review that has cost taxpayers millions. That is millions that could have delivered real relief but instead went to consultants. And what has it delivered? Nothing but uncertainty, and not a cent of meaningful benefit to motorists. Then came the chaos of announcing the end of the $60 weekly toll cap without any clear replacement. Motorists were left confused and anxious. And now, after all that, what is Labor's big idea? New tolls, higher tolls, two-way tolls.

This is not a solution; it is desperation driven by financial mismanagement. The people of Willoughby and the people of New South Wales should not be forced to pay for this Government's budget failures. They should not be punished for Labor's inability to manage money. And they should not have to carry the cost of a broken promise. Any move towards two‑way tolling is a new toll. It breaks their promise, plain and simple, and it adds to the crushing financial pressures families are already facing. That is the reality. I will stand with motorists, commuters, families, workers and small businesses who rely on the Harbour Bridge and Sydney Harbour Tunnel every day, whether they live in Willoughby or beyond. The people of New South Wales deserve honesty and integrity. They deserve transparency. And they deserve a fair go. Most of all, they deserve a government that does not see them as a source of endless toll revenue.

The House adjourned, pursuant to resolution, at 18:54 until

Friday 21 November 2025 at 10:00.

tree_branches.text: Mr RAY WILLIAMS ( Kellyville ) —I'm pleased to acknowledge the opening of the new Return and Earn Depot at Hare Place, Rouse Hill. This large-format facility makes it even easier for Hills residents to participate in the scheme, particularly those returning high volumes of containers, thanks to its fast "tip and go" self‑service system. Its convenient operating hours—7am to 6pm, seven days a week—make it even more accessible for the community. I'm extremely proud to have been part of the former Coalition Government that launched this initiative in December 2017, despite resistance from Labor at the time. Return and Earn has since grown into Australia's most successful litter-reduction program, outperforming all other environmental initiatives nationwide. The results speak for themselves: more than 14.6 billion containers returned, a 65% drop in drink-container litter, 83% community participation, and over 1.2 million tonnes of materials recycled. The scheme has also delivered an impressive $82 million to charities and community organisations through donations and handling fees. Congratulations to TOMRA for rising to the challenge and exceeding expectations.

tree_branches.name: Bankstown Sports Group - $1m In Clubgrants to Local Organisations
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Bankstown Sports Group - $1m In Clubgrants to Local Organisations
tree_branches.text: Mr JIHAD DIB ( Bankstown — Minister for Custome r Service and Digital Government, Minister for Emergency Services, and Minister for Youth Justice ) —I would like to congratulate Bankstown Sports Group for continuing to demonstrate its deep commitment to our community. Through the 2024–2025 ClubGRANTS program, Bankstown Sports Group has provided over $1 million in funding across three Local Government Areas. This year, more than 50 local organisations have received vital support, enabling them to deliver services that make a real and lasting difference. From healthcare and youth development to food security and social support, these grants address a wide range of community needs. Over $200,000 was provided to Bankstown-Lidcombe Hospital for nurse training, cancer diagnosis equipment, and dementia support, with more than $100,000 supporting youth programs across the region. Targeted initiatives include funding to organisations across various social programs. These include 777 Movement Ltd for their Homeless to Home program, The Salvation Army Villawood Hub, Humanity Matters Inc for children's psychological assessments, and St Francis Social Services for refugee employment pathways. Through ClubGRANTS, Bankstown Sports Group proudly backs the organisations that uplift and empower our Bankstown community. Thank you for playing a vital role in enabling community organisations to drive meaningful change and improve lives across Bankstown.

tree_branches.name: Mr JIHAD DIB
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Bankstown Sports Group - $1m In Clubgrants to Local Organisations > Mr JIHAD DIB

tree_branches.name: Indigenous Elder Uncle John
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Indigenous Elder Uncle John
tree_branches.text: Mr JIHAD DIB ( Bankstown — Minister for Customer Service and Digital Government, Minister for Emer gency Services, and Minister for Youth Justice ) —I am honoured to acknowledge and celebrate Indigenous Elder Uncle John Dickson for his outstanding achievement in receiving the 2025 Male IFEFA Pride of Australia Advocacy Award at the International Film and Entertainment Festival Australia Curtain Raiser Event, held in NSW Parliament. For more than two decades, Uncle John has stood with a deep sense of pride for our community, sharing Indigenous stories and culture through his art. He began his journey as the Indigenous Elder representative at community gatherings, offering Welcome to Country and leading smoking ceremonies with deep respect and cultural strength. Over the years, his contributions have grown to embrace not only Indigenous culture, but the rich diversity of all cultures within our community. From partnering with the local PCYC to support at‑risk young people through art and meditation, to recently becoming the first Elder in our community to formally welcome newly arrived Palestinian refugees to Australia - his leadership continues to uplift and connect us all. Uncle John, your dedication to nurturing our community is inspiring. I extend my heartfelt thanks to you, and to Aunty Liz, for your tireless advocacy, generosity, and steadfast support of our Bankstown community.

tree_branches.name: Mr JIHAD DIB
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Indigenous Elder Uncle John > Mr JIHAD DIB

tree_branches.name: The Wise Up: Empowering Youth and Community Program
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > The Wise Up: Empowering Youth and Community Program
tree_branches.text: Mr JIHAD DIB ( Bankstown — Minister for Customer Service and Digital Government, Minister for Emergency Services, and Minister for Youth Justice ) —I recently had the pleasure of attending the Wise Up: Empowering Youth and Community Program, proudly supported by the Campsie Police Area Command. This outstanding initiative focuses on helping young people build confidence and leadership skills through goal setting, teamwork, and personal development—empowering students to achieve their best both in and beyond the classroom. It was wonderful to meet and speak with students from Bankstown Girls High School and Unity Grammar, who shared their aspirations and the positive impact the program has had on their motivation and self‑belief. Their enthusiasm and determination were inspiring and a reflection of the program's success in fostering resilience and community connection among young people. A special thank you to Ali Faraj from the GWS Giants and Jamal Rifahi empowering, encouraging and reminding the students that with focus and perseverance, anything is possible. Gratitude also goes to our local NSW SES Canterbury Unit for generously providing their venue and ongoing support for youth engagement initiatives. Programs like Wise Up remind us of the importance of investing in our young people—empowering them to grow, lead, and contribute to a stronger, more connected community.

tree_branches.name: Macquarie Fields Men's Shed
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Macquarie Fields Men's Shed
tree_branches.text: Mr ANOULACK CHANTHIVONG ( Macquari e Fields — Minister for Better Regulation and Fair Trading, Minister for Industry and Trade, Minister for Innovation, Science and Technology, Minister for Building, and Minister for Corrections ) —The Macquarie Fields Men's Shed is a thriving hub for companionship and purpose. The shed has been at its spacious new location at Macquarie Reserve for two years, enabling the group to flourish and supporting the development of a bountiful vegetable garden. More recently, the shed completed a project to build 40 wooden crosses for Bardia Public School's Memorial Garden for commemoration ceremonies such as ANZAC Day. For more than 10 years, the Men's Shed has supported Operation Christmas Child through the charity Samaritan's Purse. This year, the men built 2,500 miniature chalkboards and wooden toy cars to be included in shoeboxes for distribution to children in need around the world. The Men's Shed recently partnered with Macquarie Fields Salvation Army to build customised donation boxes in the lead-up to Christmas. Offering a safe space for men from all walks of life to connect, the Macquarie Fields Men's Shed fosters friendships, knowledge-sharing, and positive relationships. I commend Phil Watt and the team at Macquarie Fields Men's Shed on their wonderful work in our community, and I look forward to many more visits.

tree_branches.name: Willoughby Girls High School Mock Election
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Willoughby Girls High School Mock Election
tree_branches.text: Mr TIM JAMES ( Willoughby ) —Willoughby Girls High School gave Year 10 Commerce students a real-world lesson in democracy through a mock election on 17 October I was proud to attend. Organised by Social Science teacher Amanda Eggleton, the program engaged more than 100 students in campaigning, debating and learning about civic participation. The event encouraged teamwork, research and respectful discussion, helping develop informed future voters and community leaders. Candidates presented concise platform speeches, answered questions and engaged with their peers on policy and values. The format mirrors a real campaign and builds skills in research, public speaking and respectful debate. I thank Ms Eggleton and the commerce teachers for their planning and guidance. I commend the student candidates for putting their ideas forward and all Year 10 students for their interest and thoughtful questions. Initiatives like this strengthen civic understanding, encourage critical thinking and help develop the next generation of informed voters and community leaders. Willoughby Girls High School has set a strong example of classroom learning connected to real-world citizenship. I congratulate the students and staff on a successful election launch and their commitment to democratic education.

tree_branches.name: Northern Suburbs Touch
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Northern Suburbs Touch
tree_branches.text: Mr TIM JAMES ( Willoughby ) —I congratulate the Northern Suburbs Touch Association on being named the Sydney Scorpions Affiliate of the Year for 2024/25. This is a significant honour that recognises strong participation, good governance and consistent results across competitions. The Association's success is built on the work of players, referees, coaches, managers, administrators and volunteers who turn up week after week. Junior pathways are thriving with growing minis and youth grades. Senior women's, men's and mixed competitions are well supported. Referee training and accreditation continue to lift standards on the park. Northern Suburbs Touch is also active beyond game day. Schools programs introduce more young people to the sport. Community carnivals and come and try days keep the door open for new participants. Representative teams compete with pride and bring experience back to local comps. Thank you to the committee and the wider volunteer base for keeping the sport accessible and organised. This award is well earned and reflects a strong culture that benefits players and families across the North Shore. Well done to everyone involved!

tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Monalisa Jani, CASS Gumnut Elc
tree_branches.text: Mr TIM JAMES ( Willoughby ) —I congratulate Monalisa Jani, Teaching Director at CASS Gumnut Early Learning Centre in St Leonards, on receiving the Director/Nominated Supervisor Excellence Award at the 2025 Excellence in Early Childhood Education Awards. This honour reflects Monalisa's steady leadership, commitment to high standards and focus on each child's wellbeing and growth. Her work lifts outcomes for children and supports families through a caring and professional service. I acknowledge the whole CASS Gumnut team for their dedication to quality practice and continuous improvement. Strong partnerships with parents and carers are a hallmark of the centre and this award is a credit to that shared effort. Monalisa's achievement is a proud moment for St Leonards and the Lower North Shore and highlights the vital contribution of early childhood educators across our community. I'm proud of you Monalisa!

tree_branches.text: Mr GREG WARREN ( Campbelltown ) —Five years ago, SWADISHT began as a humble dream, today, it stands as a vibrant celebration of unity, culture, and community. SWADISHT 2025 was more than a festival; it was a heartfelt reminder of what makes Campbelltown truly special. To Shefali and the Alkalizer team, your vision, dedication, and love have created something extraordinary. You've built a space where traditions are honoured, diversity is celebrated, and community thrives. This event has quickly become a staple of our Campbelltown calendar, and I have truly marvelled in watching it go from strength to strength. Once again, congratulations to Shefali and the numerous others who were involved in every step of ensuring that the night went as perfectly as it did. I can't wait to be back again next year.

His success, supported by Model Mates and the Autism Mates charity, highlights the importance of creating opportunities for people of all abilities to shine. Richard's big moment reminds us of the power of community support and the incredible potential that thrives when everyone is given a chance to belong.

tree_branches.text: Dr MARJORIE O'NEILL ( Coogee ) —We acknowledge and support the upcoming Coogee Island Challenge on 30 November 2025, an event that continues to bring our community together through fitness, fun and ocean appreciation. tree_branches.name: Professor Phil Morgan - Daughters and Dads
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Professor Phil Morgan - Daughters and Dads
tree_branches.text: Ms SONIA HORNERY ( Wallsend ) —The University of Newcastle's Daughters & Dads Active and Empowered program, created by Professor Phil Morgan, Deputy-Director of the Priority research Centre for Physical Activity and Nutrition and father of 3 daughters, was honoured at the Engagement Australia 2025 Excellence Awards in Sydney on 12 November 2025 at the Refectory, University of Sydney with the Outstanding Engagement for Research Impact Award. Professor Morgan's work focuses on the essential role that fathers play in their children's development. His programs have garnered 18 national and international research excellence awards and have been adapted around the world. More than 7,000 participants have experienced Daughters & Dads since its inception in 2015, where dads and their daughters enjoy sessions focusing on physical activity, playing sports like basketball, cricket and football. Professor Morgan says that a strong connection between fathers and their daughters is associated with a plethora of enhanced outcomes for girls, including better confidence, self-esteem, resilience and sporting ability. Congratulations on your award. I am sure that your programs will continue to have a significant impact for communities across Australia and the globe.

tree_branches.name: Sophie Gladman
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-11-20) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Sophie Gladman
tree_branches.text: Ms SONIA HORNERY ( Wallsend ) —At the Hunter Academy of Sport awards evening, Wednesday 22 October 2025 at McDonald Jones Stadium, Waratah resident Sophie Gladman,16, was named Sailing Rising Star, recognised for outstanding dedication and performance in the sailing program. With other athletes, coaches and volunteers, Sophie was celebrated for her hard work, dedication and success throughout the year. Sophie has been involved in the sport since the age of 6, currently sailing an Elliot 6 SuperSport boat at the Newcastle Cruising Yacht Club [NCYC]. Her dad Rohan and sailing instructors Andrew Omotosho and Tom Farley have been important influences. In fact, everyone in Sophie's family has sailed, so it is second nature to her. She enjoys the teamwork of the sailing community. The NCYC Youth Squad involves both on and off-water sessions, racing regatta experience and skill development in advanced keelboat handling skills, fleet race training, racing rules and teamwork dynamics. Sophie has been an assistant instructor for Tackers and, in the Christmas holidays, plans on doing a keelboat instructor course. She dreams of racing around the world, hoping to experience many different places and racing environments. Congratulations, Sophie!
